title: Choosing the right material for a job

summary.text: Why is a kadhai made of metal, but its handle of wood or plastic? Metal carries heat to the food fast, and wood and plastic carry it to your hand only slowly. A property is what a material is like, such as hard, bendy, waterproof or see-through, and we choose a material because its properties suit the job. Most objects are made of several materials, each doing the job it suits best. In this unit you test spoons, woollen socks and clay pots to find out which material does which job, and why.
summary.art: A kitchen shelf with a steel kadhai with a wooden handle, a clay matka, a woollen tea cosy and a plastic raincoat on a hook, each with a small label arrow pointing to the part that does its job.

intro.hook: Try this. Imagine a kadhai made of chocolate, an umbrella made of paper and a chappal made of glass. What would go wrong with each one?
intro.text: Somebody chose the material of every object in your home. They chose steel for your tumbler, cotton for your kurta and plastic for your bucket, because each suits its job. Some choices are surprising. Water left in a clay pot stays cooler than water left in a steel bottle in the same room. A woollen sweater does not make any heat at all. In this unit you test materials the way an engineer does, and find out why each one is right for its job.
intro.art: A child holding a chocolate kadhai that is melting on a stove, a paper umbrella going soggy in the rain, and a glass chappal with a crack, all drawn as a funny three-panel cartoon.

outcomes: I can explain that we choose a material for a job because of its properties, and give examples from my home.
I can say why a pan is made of metal and its handle of wood or plastic, using the words conductor and insulator.
I can explain why a sweater, a clay matka and a flask work, using the ideas of trapped air and evaporation.
I can explain why most things are made of several materials, each doing one job.
I can spot a silly choice of material and suggest a better one, thinking about cost, weight, safety and the Earth.
I can run a test to choose the best material for a job, record my results in a table and a chart, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that a material's properties come from its atoms, and give examples of clever materials made by living things and used in spacecraft.

terms.meaning: What an object is made of.
terms.example: Your tumbler is made of steel. Your kurta is made of cotton.
terms.art: A steel tumbler and a cotton kurta, each with a label showing its material.

terms.meaning: A thing you can see and touch. One object can be made of one material or many.
terms.example: A pencil is one object made of wood, graphite, paint and sometimes a rubber eraser.
terms.art: A pencil cut open to show its wood, its grey lead and its eraser.

terms.meaning: What a material is like, or what it can do. Hard, soft, bendy, waterproof and see-through are all properties.
terms.example: Glass is see-through. Rubber is stretchy. Cotton soaks up water.
terms.art: Three small pictures: light shining through glass, a rubber band stretching, a cotton towel soaking up a spill.

terms.meaning: The job a material does in an object.
terms.example: Glass is used for windows because you can see through it.
terms.art: A window with sunlight streaming through, a child looking out.

terms.meaning: A material that lets heat pass through it quickly. Most metals are good conductors of heat.
terms.example: A steel spoon left in hot chai gets hot all the way up to the end.
terms.art: A steel spoon in a cup of chai with warm red colour creeping up the handle.

terms.meaning: A material that lets heat pass through it only slowly. Wood, plastic, wool, cork and air are good insulators.
terms.example: A wooden spoon left in hot dal stays cool at the end you hold.
terms.art: A wooden spoon in a pot of dal, the handle end shown cool blue.

terms.meaning: Does not let water through.
terms.example: A plastic raincoat is waterproof, so you stay dry in the monsoon.
terms.art: Raindrops bouncing off a plastic raincoat.

terms.meaning: Soaks up water or other liquids.
terms.example: A cotton towel is absorbent. It soaks up the water on your skin.
terms.art: A cotton towel drinking up a puddle of water.

terms.meaning: Bends easily without breaking.
terms.example: A rubber chappal is flexible. It bends as you walk.
terms.art: A rubber chappal bending in two hands.

terms.meaning: Stiff. It keeps its shape and does not bend easily.
terms.example: A wooden table is rigid, so your plate stays flat on it.
terms.art: A wooden table holding a plate, perfectly flat.

terms.meaning: Hard to break, tear or snap.
terms.example: Steel is strong, so it is used for bridges and almirahs.
terms.art: A steel bridge over a river with a train crossing.

terms.meaning: Hard, but it cracks or shatters when hit or bent.
terms.example: A glass bangle is brittle. It breaks if it falls on a stone floor.
terms.art: A glass bangle cracking into pieces on a stone floor.

terms.meaning: Lasts a long time, even when used again and again.
terms.example: A steel thali can be used every day for years. A paper plate is used once.
terms.art: An old shiny steel thali next to a crumpled paper plate.

terms.meaning: Full of tiny holes, called pores, that water or air can move through.
terms.example: A clay matka is porous. Water slowly seeps through it to the outside.
terms.art: A zoom into the wall of a clay pot showing tiny tunnels with water seeping through.

terms.meaning: When a liquid slowly turns into a gas and goes into the air. Evaporation takes heat away, so it cools things down.
terms.example: Wet clothes dry on the line because the water evaporates. Your wet skin feels cool in a breeze.
terms.art: Clothes drying on a line with faint wisps of water rising into the air.

terms.meaning: A material made by joining two or more materials, so it has good properties of each.
terms.example: Plywood is thin sheets of wood glued together. Bone is a natural composite of a bendy part and a hard part.
terms.art: A piece of plywood showing its layers, beside a bone cut open.

terms.meaning: A material made by people, mostly from oil and gas. It is made of very long chains of atoms joined together. Plastics can be shaped into almost anything.
terms.example: Buckets, toothbrushes and pen bodies are usually plastic.
terms.art: A bucket, a toothbrush and a pen, and a zoom showing long tangled chains like noodles.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that every material is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Your steel spoon is mostly iron atoms, packed together very tightly.
terms.art: A zoom from a steel spoon down to rows of tiny packed balls.

terms.meaning: An even tinier particle on the outside of every atom. In metals, some electrons are free to move about, which is why metals carry heat and electricity so well.
terms.example: When one end of a steel spoon gets hot, its free electrons carry the heat along to the other end.
terms.art: Rows of metal atoms with tiny dots zipping freely between them.

terms.meaning: A person who designs and builds things to solve problems. Choosing materials is a big part of an engineer's job.
terms.example: An engineer chooses steel and concrete for a bridge, and rubber for its joints.
terms.art: A woman engineer in a hard hat holding a drawing of a bridge with labels for steel and rubber.

terms.meaning: Copying the clever designs of living things to make new materials and machines.
terms.example: Water rolls off a lotus leaf. Scientists copied it to make paints that clean themselves.
terms.art: A drop of water rolling off a lotus leaf, and the same drop rolling off a painted wall.

explanations.definition: We choose a material for a job because its properties suit that job. The job says what properties are needed. Then we look for a material that has them.
explanations.description: Think of a raincoat. Its job is to keep you dry. So it needs a material that is waterproof. It must also be flexible, so you can move your arms. Plastic and rubber-coated cloth have both properties. A towel has a different job. It must soak up water, so it needs an absorbent material, like cotton. The same property can be good for one job and bad for another. Soaking up water is perfect for a towel and terrible for a raincoat.
examples: A window is glass because glass is transparent, so light comes in and you can see out.
A cricket bat is willow wood because it is strong but not too heavy, and it does not shatter.
An electric wire is copper inside, because copper carries electricity well. Its cover is plastic, because plastic stops electricity from reaching your hand.
explanations.art: A raincoat and a towel side by side, with raindrops bouncing off one and soaking into the other.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: we pick a material because of what it is like.

explanations.concept: One job, many materials. One material, many jobs.
explanations.definition: The same job can often be done by several materials. And one material can do many different jobs.
explanations.description: Look at spoons. People make them from steel, wood, plastic, silver, coconut shell and even bamboo. Each one works, because each is rigid and can be shaped into a bowl. But each has extra good and bad points. A steel spoon is durable and easy to clean. A wooden spoon does not scratch a non-stick pan. A coconut-shell spoon is cheap and goes back into the soil when it is thrown away. Now look at steel. It makes spoons, almirahs, bridges, cycle frames and needles. Steel is strong, so it suits all of them.
examples: Plates can be steel, banana leaf, areca palm leaf, paper, clay or plastic.
Cotton makes kurtas, towels, bedsheets, wicks for diyas and the cotton wool in a first-aid box.
Bamboo makes houses, baskets, flutes, ladders and scaffolding.
explanations.art: A fan of spoons made of steel, wood, plastic, coconut shell and bamboo, and beside it a steel spoon, a steel almirah and a steel bridge.
explanations.context: This card shows two surprises: many materials can do the same job, and one material can do many jobs.

explanations.concept: There is no best material, only the best for this job
explanations.definition: No material is best at everything. Choosing a material means weighing up what matters most for the job: how well it works, cost, weight, safety, how long it lasts and what happens to it afterwards.
explanations.description: Engineers call this a trade-off. You give up a little of one thing to get more of another. Steel is very strong but heavy. Aluminium is weaker but much lighter, so it is used for aeroplanes and pressure cookers. Glass is wonderfully clear but brittle, so spectacles are often made of plastic instead, which is lighter and does not shatter. A banana leaf makes a lovely plate for a feast, and it rots away after. But you cannot keep it for next week. The best choice depends on the job, the place and the person.
examples: Spectacles for a small child are often plastic, because a fall would shatter glass.
A bamboo house can bend in an earthquake, while a brick wall with nothing holding it together may crack.
A steel tiffin costs more than a plastic box, but it lasts for many years.
explanations.art: A balance scale with 'strong' on one side and 'light' on the other, a steel bar and an aluminium bar on the pans.
explanations.context: Is steel the best material? Is plastic? This card explains why the answer is always: best for what?

explanations.concept: Silly materials, and what goes wrong
explanations.definition: A material is a silly choice when one of its properties stops the object from doing its job.
explanations.description: Silly objects are a good way to think. A chocolate teapot would melt, because chocolate turns soft when it is warm. A paper umbrella would go soggy and tear, because paper is absorbent and weak when wet. A glass chappal would crack, because glass is brittle. A wool swimming costume would soak up water and sag. Each time, ask two questions. Which property is the problem? Which material has the property we need?
examples: A cardboard boat would soak up water and sink, unless it is coated with wax.
Ice spectacles would melt on your nose.
A steel pillow would be far too hard and rigid.
explanations.art: A funny cartoon of a chocolate teapot melting, a paper umbrella flopping, and a glass chappal cracked.
explanations.context: This card uses funny made-up objects to show how one wrong property can ruin a design.

explanations.concept: Pans and handles: conductors and insulators
explanations.definition: A conductor of heat lets heat pass through it quickly. An insulator lets heat pass through only slowly. Most metals are good conductors. Wood, plastic, cloth, cork and air are good insulators.
explanations.description: A kadhai must carry heat from the flame to the food, fast and evenly. So it is made of a metal, like iron, steel or aluminium. But the handle must keep heat away from your hand. So it is made of wood or a special hard plastic, which are insulators. The Hot Spoon Race in this unit shows the difference. Butter stuck on the handle of a steel spoon standing in hot water melts within a few minutes. Butter on a wooden spoon stays solid. Many pressure cookers have metal bodies and plastic handles for exactly this reason.
examples: A tawa is iron. Its handle is often wood.
A steel tumbler of hot chai is too hot to hold. A clay kulhad of the same chai is easy to hold.
Oven gloves are thick cloth with air trapped inside, which is a good insulator.
explanations.art: A pressure cooker cut in half: red heat arrows rushing through the metal pot, blue arrows stopping at the plastic handle.
explanations.context: Why is a pan metal but its handle wood or plastic? This card explains, using the Hot Spoon Race.

explanations.concept: A sweater does not make heat
explanations.definition: Wool, cotton wool and feathers keep things warm because they trap lots of still air. Still air is a very good insulator. They do not make any heat themselves. They only slow heat down as it tries to escape.
explanations.description: Your body makes heat all the time. Without a sweater, that heat leaks away into the cold air. A sweater is full of tiny pockets of air between its curly fibres. The trapped air cannot move about, so heat passes through it very slowly. So your own heat stays near you. Here is the surprise. Wrap an ice cube in a woollen sock and it melts more slowly than an ice cube left in the open. The sock keeps the room's heat out, just as it keeps your body's heat in. Insulators slow heat down in both directions.
examples: An ice cube inside a woollen sock stays frozen longer than one on a bare plate.
A quilt, a razai, is thick with cotton and air, so it keeps you warm on winter nights.
Birds fluff up their feathers on cold mornings, to trap more air.
explanations.art: A zoom into a woollen sweater showing curly fibres with little pockets of air, and an ice cube peeping out of a woollen sock.
explanations.context: Many people think a sweater makes you warm by itself. This card explains what it really does, using the sweater and ice cube test.

explanations.concept: Why a clay matka keeps water cool
explanations.definition: A clay matka is porous. Water seeps slowly through its tiny holes to the outside. There it evaporates, and evaporation takes heat away from the pot and the water inside.
explanations.description: When a liquid evaporates, it needs heat to turn into a gas. It takes that heat from whatever it is touching. That is why you feel cool when you come out of a bath and stand in a breeze. A matka works the same way. Its outside is always a little damp. As that water evaporates, it takes heat from the pot. So the water inside stays cooler than the air. It works best in dry, breezy weather. In very damp, sticky weather, water evaporates slowly, so the matka cools less. A plastic or steel bottle has no pores, so this cannot happen.
examples: In hot Indian summers, families have kept drinking water in clay matkas and surahis for thousands of years.
A wet cloth wrapped round a steel bottle in a breeze makes the water cooler, because the cloth's water evaporates.
Mansukhbhai Prajapati, a potter from Wankaner in Gujarat, used the same idea to make a whole clay fridge that needs no electricity. He called it Mitticool.
explanations.art: A clay matka sweating tiny droplets on its outside, with wavy lines rising into the air and a blue cool glow inside.
explanations.context: A clay pot can keep water cooler than the air around it. This card explains how, using the Matka Mystery test.

explanations.concept: Most objects are made of several materials
explanations.definition: Most objects are made of several materials. Each material does the job its properties suit best.
explanations.description: No single material can do everything, so designers put materials together. An umbrella has waterproof cloth to keep off rain. It has springy steel ribs to hold the cloth open. It has a plastic or wooden handle that is comfortable to hold. A pencil has soft graphite to leave a mark, wood to hold it and protect it, and paint so the wood does not get dirty. Sometimes two materials are joined so closely that they become a new material, called a composite. In 1823, a Scottish chemist, Charles Macintosh, made waterproof cloth by gluing two layers of cloth together with rubber in the middle. The cloth made it soft. The rubber made it waterproof. In Britain, a raincoat is still sometimes called a mackintosh, or a mac.
examples: A bicycle uses steel for the frame, rubber for the tyres, leather or plastic for the seat, and oil to help the chain move.
A kurta button can be plastic, wood, coconut shell or metal, sewn on with cotton thread.
A school bag uses strong cloth, plastic zips, foam padding for your back and a waterproof lining.
explanations.art: An open umbrella with labelled arrows: waterproof cloth, springy steel ribs, plastic handle.
explanations.context: Look around: almost nothing is made of just one material. This card explains why, with umbrellas, pencils and the first raincoat.

explanations.concept: Deep down, properties come from atoms
explanations.definition: A material's properties come from what its atoms are and how they are joined together.
explanations.description: Zoom into a steel spoon until you see its atoms. They are packed in neat rows. Some of their electrons, the tiny particles on the outside of atoms, are not stuck to any one atom. They wander freely through the whole metal. When one end gets hot, these free electrons carry the energy along very fast. They also make metals shiny, because they bounce light back. Now zoom into wood or plastic. Their electrons are held tightly in place, so heat creeps through slowly. Plastic is made of very long chains of atoms tangled like noodles. That is why many plastics can bend. Cotton is a mat of fibres with gaps between them. Water creeps into the gaps, so cotton is absorbent.
examples: Metals are shiny, carry heat and bend without snapping, all because of their free electrons and their neat rows of atoms.
Rubber is stretchy because its long chains are curled up. Pulling straightens them. Letting go lets them curl back.

Diamond and pencil lead are both made of carbon atoms. In diamond they hold each other tightly in every direction, so it is the hardest natural material. In pencil lead they form flat sheets that slide, so it is soft.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a steel spoon, a shiny surface, rows of atoms, tiny electrons zipping freely between them.
explanations.context: This card zooms in far past what any eye can see, to find out where a material's properties really come from.

explanations.definition: Living things make materials with amazing properties, at ordinary temperatures, from simple things like water, sugar and minerals. Copying them is called biomimicry.
explanations.description: Bone is a composite. It mixes a bendy material called collagen with a hard mineral. The mineral alone would be brittle like chalk. The collagen alone would bend like rubber. Together, they make bone hard and tough. A lotus leaf stays clean in muddy ponds. Its surface is covered in tiny waxy bumps, so water rolls off in balls and carries the dirt away. In 1997, two German botanists, Wilhelm Barthlott and Christoph Neinhuis, explained this and called it the lotus effect. Now some paints and glass use the same trick. Spider silk is light, stretchy and very tough. Scientists have tried for years to make it in factories, using bacteria, yeast and even goats.
examples: The shiny inside of a seashell, called mother-of-pearl, is made of tiny flat tiles of mineral glued with a bendy material, like bricks and cement.
Your tooth enamel is the hardest material in your body.
Velcro was invented after a Swiss engineer, George de Mestral, looked closely at burrs stuck to his dog's fur.
explanations.art: A lotus leaf with water rolling off as balls, a spider web with dew, and a bone cut in half showing its inside.
explanations.context: People are not the only inventors of materials. This card shows how living things make clever materials, and how we copy them.

explanations.definition: Space is airless, very hot in sunlight and very cold in shadow. So spacecraft need materials chosen very carefully, each for one job.
explanations.description: Many spacecraft are wrapped in a shiny gold or silver blanket. It is many thin layers of plastic coated with metal, with gaps between them. The shiny layers reflect the Sun's heat. The gaps stop heat from passing through. India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, which landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023, wore a blanket like this. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, has mirrors made of a light metal called beryllium. Beryllium keeps its shape even when it is extremely cold. The mirrors are coated with a layer of gold far thinner than a hair, because gold reflects the kind of light the telescope looks for. Some spacecraft also use aerogel, a solid so light it is mostly air. It is one of the best insulators ever made.
examples: A NASA spacecraft called Stardust used aerogel to catch tiny grains of comet dust and bring them back to Earth in 2006.
Space suits have many layers. One holds air in, some reflect heat, and the outer layer stops sharp dust from cutting through.
Rocket nozzles are made of materials that can stand fiercely hot gas rushing through them without melting.
explanations.art: A Moon lander wrapped in a crinkly gold blanket, and a giant telescope with gold hexagon mirrors floating in space.
explanations.context: In space, a wrong material can end a mission. This card shows how engineers choose materials for the hardest jobs of all.

explanations.description: Plastic is cheap, light, waterproof and can be shaped into anything. That is why it is everywhere. But it is also durable, and that is the problem. Most plastics take a very long time to break down. So thrown-away plastic piles up in fields, rivers and the sea. People disagree about what to do.
examples: Plastic drips, gloves and syringes in hospitals keep medicines clean and stop germs spreading.
Plastic bags blown into drains can block them and make floods worse in the monsoon.

perspectives.explanation: Most plastic things are used once and thrown away. Ban the ones we do not really need, like thin carry bags and straws. India banned many single-use plastic items in 2022.

perspectives.who: People who want better recycling and reuse
perspectives.explanation: Plastic does useful jobs that other materials do badly. Keep it, but use it many times, collect it properly and recycle it.
Invent plastics that last while we need them, then break down safely. This is hard. Some plastics labelled 'compostable' only break down in hot factory compost, not in a garden.

explanations.art: A balance with a hospital drip and a raincoat on one side and a plastic-choked drain on the other.
explanations.context: Plastic does many jobs well, and it also causes a big problem. This card gives the main views on what to do.

explanations.concept: Your spoon was made in a star
explanations.description: Every material on Earth is made of atoms. Where did the atoms come from? Scientists agree on most of the story. The lightest atoms, hydrogen and helium, were made just after the universe began. Heavier atoms, like the carbon in wood and the oxygen in water, were made inside stars, which squeeze small atoms together. Iron, the main atom in your steel spoon, was made in stars and in the explosions of stars. The explosions scattered these atoms into space. Later, the Sun and the Earth formed from that dust. For the very heaviest atoms, like gold, scientists still argue.
examples: The iron in your blood and in your steel tumbler was once inside a star.
The calcium in your bones was made in stars too.

perspectives.who: Many astronomers, for a long time
perspectives.explanation: Gold was made mainly when giant stars exploded. These explosions are called supernovas.

In 2017, telescopes watched two neutron stars crash together. A neutron star is the small, very heavy core left after a giant star explodes. The crash seemed to make heavy atoms like gold. So much of the gold on Earth may come from crashes like this.
Both kinds of event probably make some gold. How much comes from each is still being worked out.

explanations.art: A steel spoon in the foreground, and behind it a giant star exploding and scattering glowing dust that becomes a little Earth.
explanations.context: This card follows the materials in your kitchen all the way back to the stars, and to a question scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Materials that are still being invented
explanations.description: Some jobs still need materials nobody has made well yet. Scientists have many ideas, and some are working in laboratories. Nobody knows yet which ones will reach our homes.
examples: Self-healing concrete: Henk Jonkers, a scientist in the Netherlands, mixed tiny living bacteria into concrete. When a crack lets water in, the bacteria wake up and make limestone that fills the crack.

DNA as a building material: Yamuna Krishnan, an Indian scientist who worked in Bengaluru and now works in Chicago, folds DNA into tiny machines. They change shape inside living cells and glow to report what is happening there.

Materials that carry electricity with no loss at all, at ordinary room temperature. In 2023, some scientists claimed to have made one, called LK-99. Other scientists tested it carefully, and it did not work. The search goes on.

perspectives.explanation: Materials that heal, grow or change shape could make houses, roads and medicines last longer and waste less.
Many exciting new materials work in a laboratory but are too costly or hard to make in large amounts. We must test every claim before we trust it.

explanations.art: A crack in a concrete wall being filled by tiny glowing bacteria, and a tiny folded DNA machine glowing inside a cell.
explanations.context: This card is about materials that scientists are still trying to invent, for jobs no ordinary material can do.

agreed.text: We choose materials for jobs because of their properties.
agreed.evidence: Every engineer and maker in the world does this. When people choose badly, the object fails, like a paper umbrella in the rain.

agreed.text: Metals are good conductors of heat. Wood, plastic, wool and still air are good insulators.
agreed.evidence: Put a steel spoon and a wooden spoon in hot water. The steel one gets hot all the way up. The wooden one stays cool at the top. Scientists have measured this for every common material.

agreed.text: Trapped air keeps things warm, or keeps them cold.
agreed.evidence: An ice cube wrapped in wool melts more slowly than one left in the open. Flasks, quilts and fur all work by slowing heat down.

agreed.text: No material is best at everything.
agreed.evidence: Strong materials are often heavy. Clear materials are often brittle. That is why almost every object is made of several materials.

agreed.text: Most plastic ever made has not been recycled.
agreed.evidence: In 2017, three scientists, Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law, added up all the plastic ever made and thrown away up to 2015. They estimated that only about 9 out of every 100 parts had been recycled.

challenging.who: Almost everyone, when they touch a steel railing and a wooden bench on a winter morning
challenging.for: The metal really does feel much colder to your hand.
challenging.against: If both have been in the same place all night, they are the same temperature. A thermometer shows it. Metal feels colder because it is a good conductor. It carries heat away from your warm hand very fast. Wood carries it away slowly, so your hand stays warm.
challenging.context: This card is about a feeling everyone has: metal feels colder than wood. Is it really colder?

challenging.claim: A sweater makes you warm by making heat.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: You feel warmer as soon as you put it on.
challenging.against: A sweater has no heat of its own. It traps your body's heat. Put a sweater on a cold stone and the stone does not get warm. Wrap an ice cube in a woollen sock and it melts more slowly, not faster.
challenging.context: This card is about what a sweater really does. The sweater and ice cube test in this unit checks it.

challenging.claim: Natural materials are always better than materials made by people.
challenging.who: Some people who care about the Earth
challenging.for: Many natural materials, like cotton, bamboo, clay and banana leaves, break down easily when thrown away. Their making often needs less energy.
challenging.against: It depends. Growing cotton can use a lot of water. Leather needs chemicals to tan it. And some made materials save lives, like plastic syringes in hospitals or steel in bridges. The best choice depends on the job, how long it is used and what happens to it after.
challenging.context: This card asks whether materials from nature are always the better choice.

challenging.claim: Harry Brearley invented stainless steel, in 1913.
challenging.who: Many books, and the city of Sheffield in England
challenging.for: Brearley, working in Sheffield, made steel with chromium in it, which did not rust. He saw it could be used for knives and forks.
challenging.against: Scientists in Germany, France and the USA were also making steels with chromium at about the same time. Some patented them first. Like many inventions, stainless steel had several inventors. Each did part of the work.
challenging.context: The steel tumblers and thalis in Indian kitchens are mostly stainless steel. This card is about who should get the credit for inventing it.

challenging.claim: Charles Martin Hall found the cheap way to make aluminium, all by himself.
challenging.for: In 1886, in the USA, Hall found a way to make aluminium cheaply, using electricity. Before that, aluminium was so costly it was used for fancy jewellery. Paul Héroult found the same way in France in the same year, on his own.
challenging.against: Hall's older sister, Julia Brainerd Hall, had also studied chemistry. She helped with his experiments and kept careful records. Historians argue about how big her part was. Her name was left out of the story for a long time.
challenging.context: Aluminium makes pressure cookers, foil and aeroplanes. This card is about who found the cheap way to make it, and who was left out.

challenging.claim: Plastic is a modern material that nature never made.
challenging.for: The plastics in our buckets and bottles were invented in the last 160 years or so. The first plastic made entirely from chemicals, not from plants or animals, was Bakelite. It was invented by Leo Baekeland in 1907.
challenging.against: Nature makes many materials of long chains, just like plastic. Rubber from trees, silk, wool, horn and the shellac made by lac insects are all natural long-chain materials. Indian craftspeople have used shellac to make bangles, toys and varnish for centuries.
challenging.context: This card asks whether plastic is really a new kind of material, or whether nature got there first.

big_questions.q: Is there a material that is best at everything? Why do you think not?
big_questions.hint: Think of something very strong. Is it also light? Is it see-through? Is it cheap?

big_questions.q: Metal feels colder than wood on a winter morning, but a thermometer says they are the same. Can your senses fool you? How do you know when to trust them?
big_questions.hint: Put one hand in cold water and one in warm water, then both in the same bowl. What do they each feel?

big_questions.q: Plastic lasts a very long time. When is lasting a long time a good thing, and when is it a problem?
big_questions.hint: Think of a steel thali you use for twenty years, and a plastic straw you use for twenty minutes.

big_questions.q: Why are metals shiny and good at carrying heat, while wood is not?
big_questions.hint: Zoom in to the atoms. What are the tiny electrons doing in each?

big_questions.q: People have used clay pots to cool water for thousands of years, long before anyone knew about evaporation. Can you know how to do something without knowing why it works?
big_questions.hint: Think of something you can do, like riding a cycle, without being able to explain it.

big_questions.q: The person who invents a material often gets the credit. What about the workers who make it, or the people who first noticed the idea?
big_questions.hint: Think of the potters who made matkas long before scientists explained them.

big_questions.q: The iron in your spoon was made inside a star. Does that change how you feel about ordinary things?
big_questions.hint: Pick up a spoon. Imagine where each of its atoms has been.

big_questions.q: Living things make bone, silk and shell without fire or factories. What can engineers learn from them?
big_questions.hint: A spider makes silk from what it eats, at the temperature of a garden. A steel factory needs huge fires.

big_questions.q: If you had to choose the materials for your own house, what would matter most to you: cost, comfort, beauty, how long it lasts, or the Earth?
big_questions.hint: Would your answer change if you lived in Ladakh, or by the sea in Chennai?

big_questions.q: Some 'wonder materials' turn out not to work when others test them. Why do scientists test each other's claims?
big_questions.hint: In 2023, some scientists said they had made an amazing new material. What happened when others tried to make it too?

story.title: The Winter the Ink Did Not Freeze
story.note: Made up. Dolma, her mother, Stanzin Sir, Abi-le and the village are imagined. The science is real. Ladakh's winters are long and very cold. Sun-warmed buildings like this really exist there, built of thick mud walls with big south-facing windows, for example the SECMOL school campus near Leh.
text: In our village in Ladakh, the winter is so cold that the river freezes and the yaks grow coats like carpets. That winter, the ink froze in my inkpot every morning. I had to hold it in my armpit for ten minutes before I could write my name.

Our school was one room with concrete walls and a tin roof. The concrete was always cold, like a stone pulled out of the river. The tin roof was the worst. When I touched the nail heads on the ceiling beam, they bit my fingers with cold. We kept on our caps, our gloves, two sweaters each and our long woollen gonchas, and still our noses ran.

Our teacher was Stanzin Sir. He was new, and young, and he came from Leh, where people have heaters. He lit the kerosene stove each morning. It filled the room with smoke and made a small warm circle around itself. The children nearest the stove coughed. The children by the window shivered. Nobody learned anything except how to be cold.

My mother's kitchen was different. It was the warmest room I knew. Its walls were thick mud bricks, as thick as my arm is long. In the afternoon the sun came through the small window and lay across the wall like a sleeping cat. In the evening, after the sun had gone, I would lean my back on that wall. It was still warm. 'How does the wall remember the sun?' I asked my mother. She laughed and said, 'Mud is slow. It takes the heat slowly and gives it back slowly.'

On the bus to the market in Leh, I noticed something else. The windows were shut and the sun poured in. My gloves came off. My cap came off. Outside, the wind was sharp as a knife. Inside the bus, behind the glass, it was almost like summer.

I told Stanzin Sir. I told him about the mud wall that remembered the sun, and about the warm bus. He listened with his head on one side. Then he said, 'Let's test it.' We took two of my mother's steel cups and filled them with the same cold water. We put both on a dark flat stone in the sun. Over one cup, we put an upside-down glass jar. After the morning, the water under the jar was much warmer. The water in the open cup was barely warmer at all. 'The glass lets the sunlight in,' said Stanzin Sir, 'and stops the warm air from blowing away.'

So we made a plan. It was the biggest plan our village had ever made for a classroom. On the sunny south wall, we would put a big window of glass. Behind it, a thick mud wall, painted dark, to drink the sunlight and store its heat, like my mother's kitchen. And under the tin roof, a deep layer of straw and sawdust.

Old Abi-le, who had lived through seventy winters, shook her head. 'Glass is cold,' she said. 'Touch a window in January. It burns your hand like ice.' She was right. I touched the bus window that week and it was freezing. But the sunlight still came through it. Glass is cold to touch, but it is clear. That was the job we needed it for.

'And straw?' said Abi-le. 'Straw is for the dzo to eat.' Stanzin Sir explained that straw is full of air, and still air is like a blanket for a house. 'Like your goncha,' he said to her. 'Your goncha is not hot. It keeps your own heat in.' Abi-le looked down at her thick woollen robe for a long time. Then she said, 'Hm.' In our village, that means yes.

The whole village came to help. Grown-ups mixed mud and straw with their feet. Others carried the bricks in a long line. We children packed sawdust into sacks for the roof. The glass came from Leh on the roof of the bus, wrapped in old blankets. We all held our breath as it was lifted down.

The first sunny morning after it was finished, I came early. The air outside was so cold that my breath made clouds. I opened the door and stepped inside. The sun was pouring through the glass onto the dark wall. The room smelled of new mud. I took off my gloves. I waited for the cold to bite my fingers. It did not.

But that night, a problem came. In the morning the room was colder than we hoped. Glass lets sunlight in, but it also lets warmth slip out in the dark. So my mother and the neighbours sewed thick curtains from old woollen blankets. At sunset, we pulled them across the glass. At sunrise, we pulled them open. Each material did its own job. The glass let the sun in. The mud kept the heat. The straw kept it from leaking up through the roof. The wool shut the window at night like an eyelid.

That February, on the coldest morning of the year, I opened my inkpot. The ink was blue and liquid and ready. I wrote my whole name, Dolma Angmo, without warming it first. Stanzin Sir did not light the stove. Nobody coughed. By the window, where I sat, the sun lay across my desk like a sleeping cat.

Abi-le came to see it. She put her old hand flat on the dark wall and held it there. 'This wall remembers the sun,' she said, as if it were her own idea. I did not mind. It was a good idea. It was everyone's.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the classroom was not warmed by burning more fuel. It was warmed by choosing each material for one job, because of its properties. Glass is transparent, so it lets sunlight in, even though it feels cold to touch. Thick dark mud soaks up heat slowly and gives it back slowly. Straw and wool trap still air, which is an insulator. They do not make heat. They keep heat from leaking away. And glass also lets heat out at night, so a woollen curtain covers it. No one material could do every job. Together they did. The story also notices whose idea it was: a child, a mother's kitchen and an old woman's doubts all helped.
ask: Why was the tin roof so cold to touch? What did the village put under it?
Abi-le said glass is cold. She was right. So why did the village still use glass?
What did the dark mud wall do with the sunlight?
Why did they need woollen curtains at night?
Dolma's idea came from her mother's kitchen and a bus. Where have you noticed something that could solve a problem?

games.title: Hire a Material
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about choosing materials for jobs. A property is what a material is like, such as waterproof or strong. Players 'hire' a material for each job and must say which property gets it the job.

printables.title: 16 job cards to cut out
items: JOB: a raincoat for the monsoon
JOB: the handle of a kadhai
JOB: a window for a bedroom
JOB: a towel after a bath
JOB: a bridge over a river
JOB: a pot that keeps water cool in summer
JOB: spectacles for a small child
JOB: a warm blanket for a winter night
JOB: the bottom of a cooking pot
JOB: a wick for a diya
JOB: a plate for a wedding feast for 500 people
JOB: a rope to pull a boat
JOB: a cover for an electric wire
JOB: a box to post a glass bangle safely

printables.title: 16 material cards, each with its main properties
items: STEEL: strong, rigid, shiny, carries heat well, waterproof, durable
WOOD: strong, rigid, does not carry heat well, floats, can rot when wet
PLASTIC: waterproof, light, can be bendy or stiff, does not carry heat or electricity, lasts a very long time
WOOL: soft, warm, traps air, flexible
RUBBER: stretchy, bouncy, waterproof, grips well
CLAY (baked): porous, rigid, brittle, does not carry heat well
PAPER: light, absorbent, easy to cut, weak when wet
COPPER: carries heat and electricity very well, bendy, shiny
BANANA LEAF: waterproof on top, flexible, rots away after use
JUTE: strong when twisted into rope, rough, rots away after use
ALUMINIUM: light, carries heat well, does not rust
BAMBOO: strong, light, flexible, grows fast
STONE: very hard, rigid, heavy, durable

rules: Cut out the job cards and the material cards. Put the job cards in a pile, face down.
Deal 4 material cards to each player. Put the rest face down as a second pile.
Turn over the top job card and read it out.
Each player chooses one of their materials for the job, and puts it face down.
Everyone turns their material over. Each player says which property makes it good for the job.
The group votes for the best choice. That player wins a 'hired' token. Silly choices that are funny but wrong get a laugh, but no token.
Everyone picks up a new material card. The player with the most tokens after all 16 jobs wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Put the job cards face down in one pile. 3. Shuffle the material cards and deal 4 to each player. 4. Put the rest in a second pile.
flow.say: Every material is looking for a job. You are the boss. For each job, you hire the best material in your hand. But you must say which property gets it the job.
flow.kid: Each material card is looking for a job. You are the boss! Look at your 4 material cards. Read the properties on each one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hire a Material. It is a card game where you choose the best material for each job, and say why.

flow.do: Play one practice round together with the job card 'the handle of a kadhai'.
flow.say: Practice round. The job is the handle of a kadhai. The kadhai gets very hot on the gas. Which material would you hire for the handle?
flow.kid: Practice job: the handle of a kadhai. The pan gets very hot. Which material should hold it? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why not copper for the handle?
good: Copper carries heat very well, so the handle would burn your hand.
The heat would travel up into your fingers.

check.q: Which material is best for the handle of a hot kadhai?
options: Copper
Wood
Aluminium
check.why: Wood does not carry heat well. It is an insulator, so the handle stays cool enough to hold. Copper and aluminium are metals. They carry heat very well, so a metal handle would get hot and burn your hand. Picking a metal usually means thinking 'strong is best', when this job needs 'stays cool'.

flow.do: 1. Turn over one job card at a time. 2. Each player chooses a material and puts it face down. 3. Turn them over together. 4. Each player gives their property reason. 5. Vote, and give a token for the best choice.
flow.say: Turn your material over. Tell us the property that makes it right for this job.
flow.kid: Read the job. Pick your best material. Put it face down. Then turn it over and say why. Say the property!
flow.parent: Good hires: raincoat, plastic or rubber, waterproof. Window, glass, transparent. Towel, cotton, absorbent. Bridge, steel, strong. Ball, rubber, bouncy. Cool water pot, clay, porous. Child's spectacles, plastic, light and does not shatter. Blanket, wool, traps air. Pot bottom, steel, copper or aluminium, carries heat. Diya wick, cotton, absorbent. Feast plate, banana leaf, waterproof on top and rots away after. Rope, jute, strong when twisted. Wire cover, plastic, does not carry electricity. Mirror, glass with shiny metal behind it, or polished steel. Bangle box, sponge, squashy. Two good answers can both win if both reasons are true.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then pick one job where two materials both worked, and talk about which you would really choose.
flow.say: For the wedding plate, banana leaf and steel both work. Which would you choose, and why?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now think of a feast for 500 people. Banana leaves or steel plates? Why?
flow.think: Is there ever only one right material for a job? What else besides the property helps you choose?

games.title: The Silly Shop
games.players: 2 to 4 players. One is the shopkeeper, the others are customers.
games.context: This is an acting game. A shopkeeper tries to sell objects made of silly materials, like a chocolate kadhai. Customers must spot what will go wrong and ask for a better material.

printables.title: 16 silly product cards
items: An ice cream spoon made of ice
A copper handle for a pressure cooker
A wax plate for hot dal

printables.title: Customer's complaint slip
items: Which material would be better, and why?

rules: The shopkeeper takes the top silly product card and tries to sell it, praising it loudly.
Each customer must say what will go wrong when they use it.
Then they must name the property that causes the problem, and a better material.
A customer who gives all three wins the card. Then a new shopkeeper takes over.
The player with the most cards at the end wins.

flow.do: 1. Choose a shopkeeper. 2. Put the silly product cards face down. 3. Give each customer a complaint slip.
flow.say: Welcome to the Silly Shop! Everything here is made of the wrong material. The shopkeeper will try to sell it to you. Your job is to find out what will go wrong.
flow.kid: Welcome to the Silly Shop! Everything here is made of the wrong material. Can you find the problem before you buy?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Silly Shop. It is an acting game about objects made of the wrong material.

flow.do: The grown-up plays shopkeeper first, selling the chocolate kadhai, to show how the game works.
flow.say: Come, come! Buy my beautiful chocolate kadhai! So shiny, so brown, and it smells delicious. Perfect for frying pakoras!
flow.kid: Listen to the shopkeeper. Would you buy a chocolate kadhai? What would happen on the gas?

check.q: What is the real problem with a chocolate kadhai?
options: It is the wrong colour
Chocolate melts when it gets warm
It is too heavy to lift
check.why: Chocolate turns soft and melts when it is warm. A kadhai sits on a flame, so it would melt straight away. A better material is iron or steel, which stays solid and carries heat to the food. Picking 'wrong colour' means looking at how it looks, not at what it does. In this game, always ask what the material does.

flow.do: 1. Take turns being shopkeeper. 2. Each shopkeeper sells one silly product with lots of acting. 3. Customers fill in a complaint slip or say their answers aloud.
flow.say: Customers, tell the shopkeeper what will go wrong. Which property is the problem? What should it be made of instead?
flow.kid: Be the shopkeeper and sell your silly product! Or be a customer. Say what goes wrong. Name the problem property. Name a better material.
flow.parent: Good answers: paper umbrella, absorbent and weak when wet, use waterproof plastic cloth. Glass chappal, brittle, use rubber. Woollen costume, soaks up water and gets heavy, use stretchy nylon. Steel pillow, too hard and rigid, use cotton stuffing. Cardboard boat, absorbent, use plastic or wood. Rubber knife, too bendy to cut, use steel. Sponge bridge, too squashy, use steel or concrete. Cotton wool helmet, too soft to protect, use hard plastic with foam inside. Copper handle, carries heat, use plastic or wood. Clay bat, brittle, use willow wood. Glass football, brittle and hard, use rubber and leather. Ice spoon, melts in the mouth, use steel. Cardboard bucket, absorbent, use plastic or steel. Tissue-paper school bag, weak and tears, use strong cloth. Wax plate, melts with hot food, use steel or a banana leaf.

flow.do: Together, invent one new silly product for the shop. Then turn it into a sensible one.
flow.say: Let's invent our own silly product. Now fix it. What would you change?
flow.kid: Invent your own silly product for the shop. Draw it. Then draw the sensible one next to it.
flow.think: Was every silly product useless? Could a 'wrong' material be right for a different job? Think of a rubber knife for a play.

worksheets.title: Why Is It Made of That? (core)

items.p: A raincoat must keep you dry. Which property does its material need most?
items.why: Waterproof means it does not let water through, so the rain stays outside. Picking 'absorbent' usually means mixing up the two words. Absorbent means it soaks water up, like a towel. That is the opposite of what a raincoat needs.
items.art: A child in a raincoat in heavy rain.

items.p: Why are windows made of glass?
opts: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out
items.why: Transparent means you can see clearly through it. Glass lets light in, and it is waterproof too. Picking 'soft' or 'bendy' usually means the child is not yet thinking about what glass is like. Glass is hard and brittle.

items.p: A material that lets heat pass through it quickly, like a steel spoon, is called a conductor of ____.
items.why: Metals are good conductors of heat. That is why a steel spoon in hot chai gets hot all the way up.

items.p: Why is the handle of a pressure cooker usually made of plastic?
opts: Plastic does not carry heat well, so the handle stays cool
items.why: The plastic used for handles is an insulator of heat. It stops the heat of the pot from reaching your hand. Picking 'melts easily' is a sensible worry. That is why handles use special hard plastics that can stand some heat.
items.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you stand a steel spoon, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon in hot water, and see which one carries heat up its handle fastest.

items.p: Sort these materials. Which are good conductors of heat, and which are good insulators?
items.why: Metals, like steel, copper and aluminium, carry heat well. Wood, wool and plastic carry heat slowly, so they are insulators.

items.p: Match each object to the property that makes its material right for the job.
items.why: Each object's job needs one main property. A towel must soak up water. A ball must bounce. A bridge must hold up heavy loads. A window must let light through. A shawl must keep your heat in.

items.p: One material can be used for many different jobs.
items.why: True. Steel makes spoons, almirahs, bridges and cycle frames. Cotton makes kurtas, towels and diya wicks.

items.p: There is only one material that can make a good spoon.
items.why: False. Spoons can be made of steel, wood, plastic, silver, bamboo or coconut shell. They all work because they are rigid and can be shaped.

items.p: A chocolate kadhai would be a silly idea. Why?
opts: Chocolate melts when it is warm
items.why: A kadhai sits on a flame. Chocolate melts when it gets warm, so the kadhai would melt. Picking 'too strong' or 'waterproof' means the property chosen does not cause any problem here. Always find the property that stops the job.

items.p: Why does a clay matka keep water cool?
opts: Water seeps through its tiny holes and evaporates, taking heat away
The matka has ice hidden in it
items.why: Clay is porous. A little water seeps to the outside and evaporates. Evaporation takes heat away, so the water inside stays cooler. Picking 'clay is cold inside' usually means the child thinks materials have their own coldness. Clay is only cooled by the evaporating water.
items.context: In the Matka Mystery test, you leave the same water in a clay pot and in a plastic bottle, side by side, and measure which stays cooler.

items.p: A material with tiny holes that water can seep through is called ____.
items.why: Baked clay, sponge and bread are porous. Glass and plastic are not.

items.p: An umbrella is made of waterproof cloth, steel ribs and a plastic handle. Why use three materials?
opts: Each material does a different job
items.why: The cloth keeps off the rain. The springy steel ribs hold the cloth open. The handle is comfortable to hold. No single material does all three jobs well. Picking 'one ran out' usually means thinking the mix is an accident. Designers choose the mix on purpose.
items.context: In the Take It Apart activity, you look at an old umbrella and find the job of each material.

items.p: Why are cooking pots usually made of metal? Use the word heat in your answer.
items.a: Metal is a good conductor of heat. It carries the heat from the flame to the food quickly. It is also strong and does not melt on the gas.
items.why: A good answer names the property, carries heat well, and links it to the job, cooking food.

items.p: Name two things in your home and the material each is made of. For each one, write one property that makes it right for the job.
items.a: Any two good examples. For example: my bucket is plastic, because plastic is waterproof and light. My bedsheet is cotton, because cotton is soft and soaks up sweat.
items.why: Any two real objects, with a true property linked to the job, are right.
items.context: In the Why Is It Made of That? hunt, you go round your home and write down what each thing is made of, and why.

items.p: Draw a kadhai on a gas flame. Label the part made of metal and the part made of wood or plastic. Write why each part is that material.
items.a: The pan part is labelled metal, because metal carries heat to the food. The handle is labelled wood or plastic, because it does not carry heat to your hand.
items.why: This shows two materials in one object, each chosen for a different property.
items.art: An empty outline of a kadhai on a gas stove.

items.p: Which is the best material for a diya wick?
opts: Cotton thread, because it soaks up oil
Plastic thread, because it is waterproof
Steel wire, because it is strong
Glass thread, because it is see-through
items.why: A wick must soak up oil and carry it up to the flame. Cotton is absorbent, so it does this well. Picking plastic usually means waterproof was taken to mean 'good'. Here waterproof is the wrong property, and plastic would also melt.

items.p: Look at the chart from the Hot Spoon Race. Which spoon carried heat fastest?
items.why: The butter on the steel spoon melted first, after only 4 minutes. So steel carried heat up the spoon fastest. Steel is a metal, and metals are good conductors. Picking 'wooden' usually means the tallest bar was read as fastest. Here a taller bar means a longer wait, so the tallest bar is the slowest.
items.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you stick a blob of butter on the handle of each spoon, just above the rim of the mug and stand the spoons in hot water. You time how long each blob takes to melt and slide.

chart.title: Minutes until the butter blob melted (made-up results)
chart.note: The wooden spoon's butter had still not melted after 15 minutes, when the test stopped.

items.p: In the Hot Spoon Race, why must the butter blobs be the same size and at the same height on each spoon?
opts: To make it a fair test, so only the spoon's material changes
items.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing, here the material. A bigger blob, or one lower down, would melt at a different time, even on the same spoon. Picking 'it does not matter' means the test could not tell us which material really carries heat best.
items.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you stick a blob of butter on the handle of each spoon, just above the rim of the mug and stand the spoons in hot water.

items.p: A woollen sock makes heat, so an ice cube wrapped in it melts faster.
items.why: False. Wool makes no heat. It traps still air, which slows heat down. So it keeps the room's warmth away from the ice, and the ice melts more slowly.
items.context: In the sweater and ice cube test, you wrap one ice cube in a woollen sock and leave another on a bare plate, and see which melts first.

items.p: Look at the chart. The ice cube in the woollen sock lasted longest. What does this show?
opts: Wool slows heat down, so the room's warmth reached the ice slowly
items.why: Wool is an insulator. It slows heat from the room reaching the ice. The same wool slows your body's heat leaving you in winter. Picking 'wool is cold' is a natural guess. But wool is not cold or hot. It only slows heat down.
items.context: In the sweater and ice cube test, you put ice cubes in different wrappings and time how long each takes to melt.

chart.title: Minutes until each ice cube melted (made-up results)

items.p: On a winter morning, a steel railing feels colder than a wooden bench next to it. Why?
opts: The steel really is much colder
Steel carries heat away from your hand faster
items.why: Both have been out all night, so they are the same temperature. Steel is a good conductor, so it pulls heat out of your warm hand quickly. That makes it feel colder. Picking 'really colder' trusts the feeling, not a thermometer. A thermometer would show them the same.

items.p: Why do the water in a clay matka and the water in a plastic bottle end up different, even in the same room?
opts: Clay is porous, so water evaporates from its outside and cools it
items.why: Water seeps through the clay's tiny holes and evaporates, which takes heat away. Plastic has no holes, so the water inside cannot evaporate through it. Picking 'plastic makes heat' is not right. Plastic does not make heat. It just cannot cool the water.
items.context: In the Matka Mystery test, you leave the same water in a clay pot and a plastic bottle side by side for three hours, then measure them.

items.p: When a liquid slowly turns into a gas and goes into the air, it is called ____.
items.why: Evaporation takes heat away. That is why wet skin feels cool in a breeze, and why a matka cools water.

items.p: Sort these jobs by the property their material needs most.
items.why: A tent and a bucket must keep water in or out. A mop and a cloth must soak water up. A tea cosy and oven gloves must slow heat down.

items.p: Spectacles for a small child are often made of plastic instead of glass. Why?
opts: Plastic is lighter and does not shatter if they fall
Plastic is more transparent than any glass
Plastic is heavier, so they stay on
items.why: Glass is clear but brittle. A small child might drop them. Plastic is clear enough, lighter and safer. This is a trade-off. Picking 'more transparent' is a common guess. Good glass is actually just as clear. The reason is safety and weight.

items.p: A banana leaf and a steel thali can both be plates. When is the banana leaf a better choice?
opts: For a big feast, because it is cheap and rots away after
For every meal for twenty years
For carrying hot dal on a train
items.why: A banana leaf is waterproof on top, cheap and rots away after use. That suits a feast for hundreds of people. A steel thali is durable, so it suits everyday meals at home for years. Picking 'cooking on the gas' means mixing up a plate's job with a pan's job.

items.p: Match each material in a bicycle to its job.
pairs: grip the road and soften bumps
shine back the light of cars at night
items.why: A bicycle is made of several materials. Each one does a job that suits its properties.

items.p: Charles Macintosh made the first rubber raincoat cloth in 1823. He put rubber between two layers of cloth. Why not just use rubber on its own, or cloth on its own?
items.a: Cloth on its own soaks up rain, so you get wet. Rubber on its own is waterproof but sticky, and uncomfortable on skin. Together, the rubber keeps the water out and the cloth makes it soft and strong.
items.why: A good answer gives one weak point of each material, and says how joining them fixes both.
items.context: In Britain, a raincoat is still sometimes called a mackintosh, after Charles Macintosh, the Scottish chemist who made the first rubber waterproof cloth.

items.p: Your friend says 'Plastic is the best material, because it is waterproof and cheap.' Give two jobs where plastic would be a bad choice, and say why.
items.a: For example: the bottom of a cooking pot, because plastic would melt on the gas. A winter blanket, because a plastic sheet traps no air and does not let sweat out. A wedding plate in a field, because plastic does not rot away.
items.why: Any two jobs where a property of plastic causes a problem are right.

items.p: Put these in order, from the best conductor of heat to the worst: wood, copper, wool, steel.
items.why: Copper carries heat best of the four. Steel is a good conductor too, but not as good as copper. Wood is an insulator. Fluffy wool, with its trapped air, is an even better insulator.

items.p: Design a lunch box that keeps food warm until lunchtime. Label at least three materials, and say what each one does.
items.a: For example: a steel box inside, which is easy to clean. A thick layer of foam or wool around it, to trap air and slow heat leaving. A cloth bag outside, with a plastic zip.
items.why: A good design uses an insulator around the food, and says the job of each material.
items.art: An empty outline of a lunch box with label lines.

items.p: After the Matka Mystery test, write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
items.a: What I think: a clay matka keeps water cooler than a plastic bottle. What I saw: after three hours, the matka water was 24 degrees and the bottle water was 29 degrees. Why: water seeped through the clay and evaporated, and that took heat away.
items.why: A full answer has a claim, evidence with numbers, and a reason using the word evaporation.
items.context: In the Matka Mystery test, you leave the same water in a clay pot and a plastic bottle side by side for three hours, then measure them with a thermometer.

items.p: Why are metals good conductors of heat?
opts: Some of their electrons can move freely and carry energy fast
items.why: In metals, some electrons are not stuck to one atom. They wander through the metal and carry energy along quickly. Picking 'always hot inside' means thinking a material can have its own heat. A spoon left in a cold room is cold.

items.p: Diamond and pencil lead are both made of carbon atoms. Why is diamond so hard, and pencil lead so soft?
opts: Their carbon atoms are joined together in different ways
Pencil lead is mixed with butter
items.why: In diamond, each carbon atom holds tightly to others in every direction. In pencil lead, called graphite, the atoms make flat sheets that slide over each other. The same atoms, joined differently, give very different properties. Picking 'more carbon' usually means thinking properties depend only on amount.

items.p: In very damp, sticky weather, a matka cools water less well. Why?
opts: When the air is already full of water, water evaporates slowly
items.why: Evaporation is slow when the air already holds lots of water. Less evaporation means less cooling. Picking 'damp weather is cold' is a guess about the weather, but sticky monsoon days are often hot. The matka needs dry, moving air to work best.
items.context: A clay matka keeps water cool because water seeps through its tiny holes and evaporates from the outside.

items.p: A space blanket on the Chandrayaan-3 lander is shiny, with many thin layers and gaps between them. What does it do?
opts: The shiny layers reflect the Sun's heat, and the gaps stop heat passing through
It makes the lander heavier, so it does not float away
It makes heat to keep the lander warm
items.why: Shiny surfaces bounce heat away. The empty gaps between layers slow heat down, a bit like the trapped air in a sweater. Picking 'makes heat' is the same mix-up as the sweater idea. The blanket makes no heat. It slows heat down.
items.context: India's Chandrayaan-3 lander landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023. Like most spacecraft, it was wrapped in a shiny blanket.

items.p: Bone is a natural composite: a bendy material and a hard mineral working together.
items.why: True. The mineral alone would be brittle, like chalk. The bendy collagen alone would bend like rubber. Together they make bone hard and tough.

items.p: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in balls and carries dirt away. What is the leaf's secret?
opts: Tiny waxy bumps on its surface
The leaf is made of plastic
items.why: The leaf is covered in tiny waxy bumps. Water touches only the tips of the bumps, so it cannot spread out. It beads up and rolls away. Scientists copied this to make self-cleaning paint. Picking 'plastic' is a fair guess because plastic is waterproof. But the secret is the bumpy waxy surface.
items.context: In the Lotus Leaf activity, you drip water onto a leaf, then onto paper rubbed with candle wax.

items.p: Copying the clever designs of living things to make new materials is called ____.
items.why: Velcro, self-cleaning paint and some swimsuits all copy living things.

items.p: In 2023, some scientists said they had made LK-99, a material that carries electricity with no loss at room temperature. What happened?
opts: Other scientists tested it, and it did not work as claimed
It is now in every phone
items.why: Scientists around the world tried to make it and test it. It did not carry electricity with no loss. This is how science checks itself. Picking 'nobody tested it' misses the most important part of science: others must be able to repeat a result.

items.p: Abi-le, in the story, said 'Glass is cold'. She was right. Why did the village still choose glass for the classroom wall?
items.a: Glass feels cold to touch, but it is transparent. It lets the sunlight in, which warms the dark mud wall. Its job was to let light in, not to feel warm.
items.why: A good answer separates how glass feels from the job it does: letting sunlight in.
items.context: In this unit's story, a Ladakh village builds a sun-warmed classroom with a glass window, a dark mud wall, a straw roof and woollen curtains.

items.p: Glass lets sunlight in by day, but lets warmth out at night. How did the village in the story solve this? Which property of wool helped?
items.a: They hung thick woollen curtains over the glass at night. Wool traps air, so it is an insulator. It slowed the warmth leaking out through the glass.
items.why: The village used several materials, and each one covered another one's weak point.
items.context: In this unit's story, a Ladakh village builds a sun-warmed classroom with a big glass window.

items.p: Which question would help an engineer most when choosing a material for a bridge?
opts: What does it need to do, and which properties does that need?
Which material is the prettiest colour?
Which material did my friend choose?
items.why: Engineers start with the job. Then they find materials with the right properties, and weigh up cost, weight and safety. Picking 'newest' is tempting. But new materials are not always better, or tested enough.

items.p: Most plastic ever thrown away has not been recycled. Should plastic be banned? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: for, thrown-away plastic lasts for hundreds of years and blocks drains and harms animals. Against, plastic does jobs nothing else does as well, like clean syringes in hospitals.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a reason for each side.

answer_chart.unit: out of every 100 parts of thrown-away plastic

data.label: Dumped in landfills or the open: about 79 out of 100

items.context: In 2017, three scientists added up what happened to all the plastic thrown away up to 2015.

items.p: People kept water cool in clay pots for thousands of years before scientists explained evaporation. What does this tell us?
opts: People can find out what works by trying and noticing, before anyone explains why
The old pots did not really work
items.why: Careful noticing and testing, over many generations, found that clay pots cool water. Later, science explained why. Both kinds of knowing matter. Picking 'science was not needed' misses that science lets us improve the idea, as in the Mitticool clay fridge.

items.p: Who should get the credit for an invention: the person who first had the idea, the person who made it work, or the person who patented it? Use stainless steel or aluminium as your example.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: many people in different countries made stainless steel at about the same time, so the credit should be shared. Julia Hall helped her brother with aluminium, so her name should be remembered too.
items.why: This links the science to fairness. There is no single right answer, but the answer should give a reason.
items.context: Several inventors made stainless steel at about the same time. Charles Martin Hall found the cheap way to make aluminium, and his sister Julia helped.

items.p: Most of the iron in your steel spoon was first made where?
opts: Inside stars, long before the Earth formed
items.why: Iron atoms were made in stars and in exploding stars, and the explosions scattered them into space. The Earth later formed from that dust. A factory only melts and mixes iron that was already here. Picking 'steel factory' is fair, because that is where the spoon was made. But the iron atoms are far older.

items.p: Draw a zoom-in of a steel spoon, as if you had a super microscope. Show the atoms, and the free electrons that carry heat.
items.a: Neat rows of round atoms, with tiny dots moving freely between them, and arrows showing heat moving along.
items.why: This shows why metals carry heat well: their free electrons move energy along quickly.

items.p: Invent a new material for a school uniform in a hot, rainy Indian city. List three properties it must have, and how you would test each one.
items.a: For example: it must be absorbent to soak up sweat, so drip water on it and time how fast it soaks in. It must dry quickly, so hang it wet and time it. It must be strong, so pull it with weights until it tears.
items.why: A good answer links each property to the job, and gives a fair test for each one.

experiments.title: The Hot Spoon Race
experiments.context: This is the Hot Spoon Race. You stick a small blob of butter on the handle of a steel spoon, a plastic spoon and a wooden spoon. Then you stand them in a mug of hot water and time which blob melts first. It shows which material carries heat best.
experiments.question: Which spoon carries heat up to your hand fastest: steel, plastic or wood?
experiments.predict: Before you start, line up the three spoons. Put the one you think will melt its butter first at the front, and the one you think will melt it last at the back. Then say why you put them in that order.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the spoon's material. Use the same size of butter blob on each spoon, at the same height, one finger-width above the rim of the mug. Stand all three spoons in the same mug of hot water at the same moment. Time them with the same clock.
results_table: Minutes until the butter melted and slid
How the top of the spoon felt after 10 minutes

materials.item: a steel spoon, a sturdy plastic spoon (a serving spoon or a baby's feeding spoon) and a wooden spoon, each long enough to stick out above the rim of the mug (a thin throwaway plastic spoon may bend in hot water)
butter or ghee straight from the fridge: one pea-sized blob for each spoon, and one more blob on a plate
3 dried peas, peppercorns or beads, pressed into the butter blobs
a steel mug, a jug or a deep bowl that will not tip over when three spoons lean in it
hot water, about as hot as fresh chai, from a kettle or heated in a pan, poured by a grown-up
a clock, phone timer or stopwatch

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and keeps the mug steady. Do not touch the spoons in the water. Use water that is hot, not boiling, and stand the mug on a flat, steady surface.

schedule.what: Guess which spoon wins. Race the three spoons in hot water. Time each blob of butter. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each spoon, as tall as the minutes it took. If a blob never melted, draw the bar to the top and write 'did not melt'.

flow.do: 1. Put the three spoons on the table. 2. Ask your child to hold each one and say how it feels. 3. Ask them to line up the spoons, from 'will melt its butter first' to 'will melt it last'.
flow.say: We are going to race these spoons. Not with legs. With heat. Which spoon do you think will carry heat up to its top fastest?
flow.kid: Look at the steel, plastic and wooden spoons. Hold each one. Which will get hot fastest at the top? Line them up.

ask.q: Why did you put that spoon first?
good: It is metal, and metal pans get hot.
Steel tumblers get hot with hot chai in them.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hot Spoon Race. You guess which spoon will carry heat fastest.

flow.do: 1. Stand the three spoons in the empty mug, handles up. 2. Put a pea-sized blob of cold butter on each handle, one finger-width above the rim of the mug. 3. Press a dried pea or a bead into each blob. 4. Put one more blob on a plate beside the mug. 5. Check all the blobs are the same size and the same height.
flow.say: The pea will fall off when the butter melts. That is our finish line. The blobs must match, so the race is fair. The blob on the plate tells us if the room alone is warm enough to melt butter.
flow.kid: Stand the spoons in the empty mug. Put a little butter on each handle, just above the rim. Push a pea into each blob. Make them all the same. Put one more blob on a plate.
flow.parent: If the blobs are different sizes, a small blob melts first anyway, and the test stops being fair. Cold butter from the fridge sticks best. Keeping the blobs above the rim keeps them out of the steam. On a very hot day, butter softens even on a plate. If the plate blob melts within 15 minutes, do the race in the coolest room, or in the early morning.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up lifts the spoons out. 2. The grown-up pours hot water into the mug until it is one finger-width below the rim. 3. Stand all three spoons back in at the same moment. 4. Start the timer. 5. Write down the time each pea falls.
flow.say: Go! Now we watch. Call out the moment a pea drops.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour the hot water. Stand the spoons in it. Start the timer. Shout when a pea falls! Write down the time.
flow.parent: Steel usually wins in 2 to 6 minutes. Plastic and wood both carry heat slowly. Often neither of their blobs melts before 15 minutes. Sometimes one melts late, softened by steam rising from the water. Stop after 15 minutes. Then let the spoons cool a little and feel the handles: the steel is warm, the wood is cool. If even the steel blob has not melted after 8 minutes, the water was not hot enough or the spoon is very thin. Try again with hotter water.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each spoon.
flow.say: Let's turn our times into a picture. A taller bar means a longer wait.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each spoon. Make it as tall as the minutes it took. The shortest bar carried heat fastest.

check.q: The steel spoon's pea fell first. What does that tell us about steel?
options: Steel is a good conductor of heat
Steel is a good insulator of heat
Steel makes its own heat
check.why: The heat from the water travelled up the steel fastest, so its butter melted first. A material that carries heat quickly is a conductor. Picking 'insulator' swaps the two words. An insulator would keep its butter solid, like the wooden spoon did.

chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until each butter blob melted
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. The wooden spoon's butter had not melted when the test stopped at 15 minutes.

flow.do: Look at a kadhai, a tawa or a pressure cooker together. Find the metal part and the handle.
flow.say: Now look at our kadhai. Which part should be like the steel spoon? Which part should be like the wooden one?
flow.kid: Look at a pan in your kitchen. Which part is like the steel spoon? Which part is like the wooden spoon? Why?
flow.think: Why are a chef's spoons for stirring hot dal often wooden?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now about steel, plastic and wood? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: steel carries heat much faster than plastic or wood. What I saw: the steel spoon's pea fell after 4 minutes, the plastic one after 14, and the wooden one never fell. Why: steel is a metal, and metals are good conductors of heat.
