experiments.title: Does a Sweater Make Heat?
experiments.context: This is the sweater and ice cube test. You wrap ice cubes in different materials, including a woollen sock, and leave one bare. Then you check which melts first. It tests a big idea: does wool make heat, or does it slow heat down?
experiments.question: If wool makes heat, an ice cube in a woollen sock should melt fastest. Does it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ice cube will melt first: the one on a bare plate, the one in foil, the one in a steel tumbler, or the one in a woollen sock? Which will last longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use ice cubes from the same tray, so they are the same size. Put them all in the same room, out of the sun, at the same time. Check them all at the same times. Change only the wrapping.
results_table: What it looked like after 30 minutes

materials.item: 4 ice cubes of the same size, from one tray
a dry woollen sock or a small piece of an old sweater. If you have no wool, use a thick towel folded into a pocket, and say so when you record it.
a square of kitchen foil
a small steel tumbler
4 small saucers or plates
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Wipe up melted water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Wrap the ice cubes, guess, and check them every 10 minutes until all have melted, which can take one to two hours. Read the explanation cards or do the Lotus Leaf activity while you wait.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each wrapping, as tall as the minutes its ice lasted.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put on a sweater or wrap a shawl around their arm. 2. Ask: why does it feel warm? 3. Write down their answer.
flow.say: Put on your sweater. Does it feel warm? Where does the warmth come from? Is the sweater making heat?
flow.kid: Put on a sweater. Do you feel warm? Where does that warmth come from? Does the sweater make it?

ask.q: Where does the warmth come from?
good: The sweater keeps my own heat in.
Any guess is fine here, if the child gives a reason. The test will check it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the sweater and ice cube test. It checks whether wool makes heat.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the dry woollen sock in your fist, then let it go. 2. Put one ice cube on a bare saucer. 3. Wrap one in foil. 4. Put one inside the steel tumbler on a saucer. 5. Push one deep inside the woollen sock and lay it on a saucer. 6. Note the time.
flow.say: Squeeze the sock. See how small it gets? Most of a sock is air, caught between the wool fibres. Now, if the sock makes heat, it should melt its ice cube fastest. Let's find out.
flow.kid: Squeeze the sock in your fist. How small does it get? Most of it is air! Put one ice cube on a plate. Wrap one in foil. Put one in the tumbler. Hide one in the sock. Note the time!
flow.parent: Children nearly always predict the sock will melt the ice fastest. Do not correct them. Let the test do it.

flow.do: 1. Every 10 minutes, look at each ice cube. 2. For the sock, gently peep inside. 3. Write down when each one has fully melted. Keep checking until all four have melted. The sock's ice can take one to two hours.
flow.say: Let's check. Which ice cube is smallest now? Which is biggest?
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, check each ice cube. Peep inside the sock. Which one is melting fastest? Which is still big?
flow.parent: Usually the bare cube melts first and the sock cube lasts much longer, often twice as long. Foil sometimes helps a little, because it is shiny. If you used a towel instead of wool, the result is the same: the towel cube lasts longer, because a thick towel also traps air.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart of how long each ice cube lasted.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each wrapping. The tallest bar lasted longest.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each wrapping. Make it as tall as the minutes the ice lasted. Which bar is tallest?

check.q: The ice cube in the woollen sock lasted longest. Why?
options: Wool makes cold
Wool traps still air, which slows heat from the room reaching the ice
Wool makes heat, but only a little
check.why: Wool is full of tiny pockets of still air. Still air lets heat pass through only slowly. So the room's warmth took longer to reach the ice. Picking 'wool makes cold' is a natural guess, but wool makes neither heat nor cold. It only slows heat down, in both directions.

flow.say: Tell me three things. Does a sweater make heat? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a sweater does not make heat. It slows heat down, coming in or going out. What I saw: the ice in the sock lasted 95 minutes, but the bare ice melted in 40. Why: the sock is mostly air, and still air slows heat down.
flow.think: So why do you feel warm in a sweater? Where does that heat really come from?

experiments.title: The Matka Mystery
experiments.context: This is the Matka Mystery test. You pour the same water into a clay pot, a plastic bottle and a steel bottle, and leave them side by side in the shade for three hours. Then you measure which water is coolest, with a thermometer.
experiments.question: Does a clay matka really keep water cooler than a plastic or steel bottle? Why?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After three hours, which will hold the coolest water: the clay pot, the plastic bottle or the steel bottle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same water, poured from one jug, at the same time. Put the same amount in each. Leave the lids off all three. Stand them side by side in the same shady, breezy place. Measure them all at the same time with the same thermometer.

materials.item: a small unglazed clay pot, matka or large kulhad, soaked in water for an hour first. If you have no clay pot, wrap a wet cotton cloth around a steel tumbler instead, and compare it with a dry tumbler.
a plastic bottle and a steel bottle, about the same size as the pot
a jug of tap water, filled an hour before, so it is the same temperature as the room
a kitchen or bath thermometer. Without one, dip a finger in one container, then quickly in the next: a difference of a few degrees can be felt.
a thin cotton cloth or hanky, for the extra test

experiments.safety: A clay pot is brittle, so carry it with two hands. Wipe up spills.

schedule.what: Fill the three containers and measure the start temperature (10 minutes). Come back after 3 hours and measure again (20 minutes).

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out how many degrees each one cooled down. Draw what the outside of the matka looked like.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a clay pot or matka. 2. Ask them to feel the outside after it has been soaking. 3. Ask why people keep drinking water in clay pots in summer.
flow.say: In many Indian homes, drinking water is kept in a clay matka in summer. People say it keeps the water cool. Is that true? And if it is, how?
flow.kid: Feel the outside of the clay pot. Is it damp? People say a matka keeps water cool. Shall we test it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Matka Mystery. You test whether a clay pot really keeps water cooler than bottles.

flow.do: 1. Pour the same amount of water from one jug into the pot, the plastic bottle and the steel bottle. 2. Measure the water in the jug with the thermometer and write it down. That is the start temperature for all three. 3. Stand them side by side in a shady place with a breeze, like a verandah or a window.
flow.say: All three start with the same water, at the same temperature. Only the container is different. That makes it fair.
flow.kid: Pour the same water into the pot and both bottles. Measure it with the thermometer. Write the number. Put them side by side in the shade.
flow.parent: Read the thermometer at eye level. If you have only a fever thermometer, do not use it in water. A cheap kitchen or bath thermometer works well.

flow.do: 1. Leave the three containers for 3 hours. 2. Then feel the outside of each one. 3. Measure the water in each with the thermometer. 4. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Feel the outside first. Which one is damp? Now let's measure.
flow.kid: Three hours later, feel the outside of each one. Which is damp? Now measure the water in each one. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Use an unglazed pot. A shiny glazed or painted pot has its pores sealed, so it cools much less. On a dry, warm, breezy day, the matka water is often 3 to 8 degrees cooler than the bottles. On a sticky monsoon day, the difference is smaller, because water evaporates slowly into damp air. Either result is good science.

check.q: The matka water was coolest, and the outside of the matka was damp. Why is it cooler?
options: Water seeped through the clay and evaporated, taking heat away
Clay is always cold
The plastic bottle made heat
check.why: Clay is porous. Water seeped through its tiny holes to the outside, then evaporated into the air. Evaporation takes heat from whatever it touches, so the pot and its water cooled. Picking 'clay is always cold' means thinking the material has its own coldness. A dry clay pot does not cool water.

flow.do: Extra test: 1. Wet the cotton hanky and wrap it round the steel bottle. 2. Leave it in the breeze for another hour. 3. Measure again.
flow.say: Can we turn the steel bottle into a matka? Let's give it a wet coat.
flow.kid: Wrap a wet hanky round the steel bottle. Leave it in the breeze for an hour. Is the water cooler now?
flow.think: Soldiers and travellers once carried water in canvas bags that were always a little wet. Why might that keep the water cool?

flow.say: Tell me three things. Does a matka really keep water cooler? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a clay matka keeps water cooler than a plastic or steel bottle. What I saw: after 3 hours, the matka water was 24 degrees and the plastic bottle water was 29 degrees. Why: water seeped out through the clay and evaporated, and evaporation takes heat away.

activities.title: Why Is It Made of That? A home hunt
activities.context: This is a hunt around your home. For each object you find, you write what it is made of and which property makes that material right for its job.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with three columns: Object, Material, Why that material
a pencil

activities.safety: Do not touch the gas, sockets or anything hot. Ask before opening cupboards.

schedule.what: Hunt for 12 objects. Write each one's material, and the property that makes it right for the job.

activities.record: Fill in at least 12 rows. Then count how many objects were made of each material, and make a tally.

flow.do: 1. Draw three columns on the paper: Object, Material, Why that material. 2. Do the first row together, with a steel tumbler.
flow.say: Somebody chose what each thing in our home is made of. Let's find out what they chose, and why that material suits the job.
flow.kid: Draw three columns: Object, Material, Why. First one: a steel tumbler. It is steel. Why? Steel is strong, waterproof and easy to clean.
flow.context: This is the first step of the home hunt. You find out what things are made of, and why.

flow.do: 1. Go room by room: the kitchen, the bathroom, the bedroom, the door. 2. For each object, your child says the material and one property that suits its job. 3. Write it down. 4. Look out for objects made of more than one material.
flow.say: What is it made of? Why that material and not another one? What would happen if it were made of something else?
flow.kid: Go from room to room. For each thing, say what it is made of. Then say why that material is right. Write it down.
flow.parent: Good finds: a bathroom mug, plastic, waterproof and does not break if dropped. A doormat, coir or rubber, rough and grips shoes. A window, glass, transparent. A pressure cooker, aluminium or steel with a plastic handle. A towel, cotton, absorbent. A door hinge, steel, strong. A pillow, cotton outside and soft stuffing inside.

flow.do: 1. Count how many objects were made of each material. 2. Make a tally. 3. Ask which material your home uses most, and why.
flow.say: Which material did we find most often? Why do you think so many things are made of it?
flow.kid: Count your objects. How many were plastic? How many steel? How many wood? Which material is used most in your home?
flow.think: Which object surprised you? Did anything use a material you did not expect?

activities.title: The Spoon and Plate Parade
activities.context: In this activity you line up spoons and plates made of different materials. You find out that one job can be done by many materials, each with its own good and bad points.

materials.item: as many kinds of spoon as you can find: steel, plastic, wooden, silver, bamboo, coconut shell
as many kinds of plate as you can find: steel thali, paper plate, banana leaf or areca leaf plate, clay or ceramic plate

activities.safety: Handle ceramic and clay plates gently, because they are brittle.

schedule.what: Line up spoons and plates. Compare their good and bad points.

activities.record: Make a table. For each spoon or plate, write one good point and one bad point.

flow.do: 1. Line up all the spoons. 2. Ask your child what all of them have in common. 3. Then ask what is different about each.
flow.say: All of these are spoons. They all do the same job. So why are they made of so many materials?
flow.kid: Line up the spoons. They all do the same job. What is the same about them? What is different?

good: To be stiff, so they don't bend.
A bowl shape to hold food.
To be safe to put in your mouth.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Spoon and Plate Parade. You compare spoons made of different materials.

flow.do: Do the same with the plates. For each, talk about cost, how long it lasts and what happens when it is thrown away.
flow.say: Which plate would you use for a wedding feast for 500 people? Which for every day for twenty years?
flow.kid: Now line up the plates. Which would you use for a big feast? Which for every day? What happens to each one when it is thrown away?
flow.parent: A banana leaf or areca leaf plate is cheap, waterproof on top and rots away. A steel thali lasts many years. A paper plate is used once and is often coated with plastic, so it may not rot easily.

flow.do: Now pick one material, steel, and list every job it does in your home.
flow.say: One job can use many materials. Can one material do many jobs? Let's count all the jobs steel does in our home.
flow.kid: Now pick steel. Find every job steel does in your home. Count them!

check.q: Spoons can be made of steel, wood, plastic or coconut shell. What does this show?
options: One job can be done by many materials
Only steel makes a real spoon
Spoons can be made of anything at all
check.why: Many materials have the properties a spoon needs: stiff, safe to eat from, able to hold a bowl shape. So many can do the job. Picking 'anything at all' goes too far. A spoon of paper or jelly would not work.

activities.title: Take It Apart
activities.context: In this activity you take apart an old, broken object, like an umbrella, a ballpoint pen or a torch. You find each material inside it, and work out the job each one does.

materials.item: an old broken umbrella, ballpoint pen, torch or chappal that nobody needs
a small screwdriver, used by a grown-up
a tray to keep the parts on

activities.safety: A grown-up uses the screwdriver. Umbrella ribs can be sharp and springy, so a grown-up holds them. Take batteries out of a torch first.

schedule.what: Take an old object apart. Find each material and its job.

activities.record: Draw the object exploded into its parts, like a puzzle pulled apart. Label each part's material and job.

flow.do: Choose the old object. Before taking it apart, ask your child to guess how many materials are inside it.
flow.say: This umbrella looks simple. How many different materials do you think it uses?
flow.kid: Look at the old umbrella or pen. How many different materials do you think are in it? Guess a number.
flow.context: This is the first step of Take It Apart. You find all the materials hiding inside one ordinary object.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up takes the object apart, piece by piece. 2. Put each part on the tray. 3. For each part, your child names the material.
flow.say: Let's find every material. What is this part made of? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to take it apart. Put each part on the tray. Name each material. Is it metal, plastic, cloth or rubber?
flow.parent: An umbrella usually has waterproof nylon or polyester cloth, steel or fibreglass ribs, a steel spring, a plastic or wooden handle and plastic tips. A ballpoint pen has a plastic body, a metal tip with a tiny ball, a plastic ink tube and a steel spring. A torch has a plastic case, a metal spring, a plastic or glass cover and a bulb or LED.

flow.do: For each part, ask: what job does it do, and what property helps? Then draw the exploded picture.
flow.say: Why is the rib steel and not plastic? Why is the cloth not cotton?
flow.kid: For each part, say its job. Why that material? Then draw all the parts spread out, with labels.

check.q: An umbrella's ribs are springy steel. Why?
options: Steel is strong and springs back after bending, so it holds the cloth open
Steel is waterproof, so it keeps rain off
Steel is light as a feather
check.why: The ribs must hold the cloth tight, and bend in the wind without snapping. Springy steel is strong and returns to its shape. Picking 'waterproof' gives a true property of steel, but it is the cloth's job to keep rain off, not the ribs'.

activities.title: The Lotus Leaf and the Waxed Paper
activities.context: In this activity you see how water rolls off a waxy leaf, such as a cabbage or lotus leaf. Then you change paper's property, from absorbent to waterproof, by rubbing it with a candle.

materials.item: a waxy leaf, such as a cabbage leaf from the kitchen, a colocasia (arbi) leaf or a lotus leaf, and a soft leaf, such as spinach or coriander
two pieces of plain paper
a white wax candle, not lit
a dropper or spoon, and a little water

activities.safety: Do not light the candle. Wash your hands after touching leaves from outside.

schedule.what: Drip water on leaves. Then wax some paper and test it.

activities.record: Draw how a water drop looked on each leaf and each paper. Write which one you would use for a paper boat.

flow.do: 1. Drip a few drops of water on the waxy leaf. 2. Tilt it gently. 3. Do the same on the soft leaf.
flow.say: Look at the drops. On which leaf do they roll like tiny marbles?
flow.kid: Drip water on the waxy leaf. Tilt it. Do the drops roll like marbles? Now try the soft leaf.

ask.q: What do the drops do on the waxy leaf?
good: They roll off and take the dust with them.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Lotus Leaf activity. You watch how water behaves on a waxy leaf.

flow.do: 1. Rub the candle hard all over one piece of paper, until it looks a little shiny. 2. Drip water on the waxed paper and on the plain paper.
flow.say: Paper is absorbent. Can we change that, like the leaf does? Let's give it a coat of wax.
flow.kid: Rub the candle hard all over one paper. Drip water on it. Now drip water on plain paper. What is different?

check.q: Why does water stay in a drop on the waxed paper?
options: Wax is waterproof, so it stops the water soaking into the paper
The candle made the paper hot
The paper became metal
check.why: Wax is waterproof. It fills the tiny gaps between the paper's fibres and covers them. So water cannot soak in, and it stays in a drop. Picking 'hot' is not right, because the candle was never lit. We changed paper's property by adding a second material.

flow.do: Talk about how people copy the lotus leaf, and how they change materials to suit new jobs.
flow.say: In 1997, two scientists in Germany explained why lotus leaves stay clean. Now some paints copy them. People also coat paper cups and cloth to make them waterproof.
flow.kid: Scientists copied the lotus leaf to make self-cleaning paint! People also coat paper and cloth to make them waterproof. Where have you seen this?
flow.think: If you could copy one thing from a plant or animal, what would you copy? What would you make with it?

activities.title: The Material Orchestra: why are bells made of metal?
activities.context: In this activity you knock on different materials and listen. Some ring, some thud. Then you work out why bells, ghungroos and gongs are metal, and why soft materials are used to make rooms quiet.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or plate, a wooden block or spoon, a plastic box, a folded cloth, a clay pot and a glass, to knock on
a steel spoon to tap with
a pillow or a thick towel

activities.safety: Tap the glass and the clay pot very gently, because they are brittle.

schedule.what: Knock on materials, sort them by sound, and play a short tune.

activities.record: Sort the materials into 'rings' and 'thuds'. Write which one you would use for a temple bell, and which for a quiet room.

flow.do: 1. Tap each material gently with the steel spoon. 2. Your child closes their eyes and guesses which one you tapped. 3. Sort them into 'rings' and 'thuds'.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Listen. Which material am I tapping? Does it ring or thud?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Listen to each tap. Guess the material! Does it ring for a long time, or thud and stop?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Material Orchestra. You listen to how different materials sound when you tap them.

flow.do: 1. Tap the steel tumbler and hold it up. Listen to the ring. 2. Tap it again and then press a folded cloth against it. 3. Put the ringing tumbler on a pillow.
flow.say: The steel keeps ringing. The cloth and the pillow stop it. Soft materials absorb sound. They soak up the shaking, a bit like a towel soaks up water.
flow.kid: Tap the steel tumbler. Listen to it ring. Now press a cloth on it. The ring stops! Soft things soak up sound.

check.q: Why are temple bells made of metal, not wood?
options: Metal rings for a long time when struck
Metal is soft
Wood is too shiny
check.why: Hard metals like bronze and brass vibrate for a long time when struck, so they ring loudly and clearly. Wood soaks up the shaking quickly, so it thuds. Picking 'metal is soft' mixes up the property. Bells are hard, and that is part of why they ring.

flow.do: Play a short tune together, using the ringing materials and the thudding ones as a drum.
flow.say: Music studios and cinema halls cover their walls with soft materials. Why do you think they do that?
flow.kid: Play a tune with the ringing things. Use the thuds as a drum! Why do cinema halls have soft walls?
flow.think: Which is better for a library: hard stone walls or soft cloth walls? Why?

activities.title: Be the Atoms: why metal passes heat on
activities.context: This is an acting game. Players stand in a line as the atoms of a spoon. They pass 'heat' along, first like the atoms of wood, then like the atoms of a metal with free electrons. It shows why metals carry heat so fast.

materials.item: a small soft ball or a rolled-up sock, to be 'heat'
a clock or phone timer
3 or more players, or teddies and cushions to make up the line

activities.safety: Jiggle gently. Do not push each other.

schedule.what: Act out heat moving through wood, then through metal.

activities.record: Draw the two lines of atoms: one passing heat by jiggling, one with free electrons running along.

flow.do: 1. Everyone stands in a line, close together. Each person is an atom of a spoon. 2. The person at the 'hot end' starts to jiggle. 3. They can only pass the jiggle by nudging the next person, slowly, one by one.
flow.say: You are the atoms of a wooden spoon. The end in the hot water starts to jiggle. Heat is the atoms jiggling. Pass it on, only by nudging the person next to you.
flow.kid: You are an atom in a wooden spoon. When the atom next to you nudges you, start jiggling. Then nudge the next one. Pass it along slowly.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Atoms. You act out how heat travels along a spoon.

flow.do: 1. Time how long the jiggle takes to reach the end. 2. Now the metal version: the atoms stand still in the line, but one free player is an 'electron'. 3. The electron grabs the soft ball, the heat, at the hot end and runs it to the far end. 4. Time it.
flow.say: Now we are a steel spoon. Steel has free electrons. They do not stay with one atom. They zoom about and carry heat with them. Run!
flow.kid: Now you are a steel spoon! One player is a free electron. Grab the heat ball at the hot end. Run it to the other end. Was that faster?

check.q: In the game, why did heat reach the end faster in the 'metal' line?
options: Free electrons carried it along quickly
The metal atoms were taller
The metal line was shorter
check.why: In metals, some electrons are free to move through the whole material. They carry energy along fast, like the runner. In wood, heat can only pass from one jiggling atom to the next, which is slow. Picking 'shorter' would make the test unfair. Keep both lines the same length.

flow.do: Talk about how this matches the Hot Spoon Race, if you have done it.
flow.say: Remember the spoons in hot water? The steel spoon's butter melted first. Now you know why. Its free electrons rushed the heat up the handle.
flow.kid: In the Hot Spoon Race, steel won. Now you know why! Its free electrons ran the heat up the spoon.
flow.think: Metals also carry electricity, using the same free electrons. Can you think of something in your home that uses copper wire?

setup.art: One child running along the line carrying a soft ball, while the others stand still.
setup.caption: 2. Now one 'free electron' runs the heat ball along, like metal.

projects.title: Build a Clay Pot Cooler
projects.context: In this 3-day project you build a pot-in-pot cooler. You put a small clay pot inside a bigger one, with wet sand between them. Evaporation keeps the inside cool, with no electricity. Then you test it on fresh coriander.

materials.item: two unglazed clay pots, one that fits inside the other with about two fingers of gap all round. If you have none, wrap a steel dabba in a thick wet cotton towel, stand it in a tray of water so the towel stays wet, and keep it in a breeze.
clean sand, enough to fill the gap (a plant nursery sells it). Without sand, pack the gap tightly with an old wet towel.
a wet cotton cloth to cover the top
water
a thermometer
2 small bunches of coriander or mint from the same batch (tomatoes change too slowly to see in 3 days)

projects.safety: Clay pots are heavy when wet and brittle. A grown-up lifts and carries them. Keep the cooler in the shade.

schedule.what: Build the cooler. Wet the sand. Put one coriander bunch inside, and the other in a bowl outside. Measure both temperatures.
Pour more water on the sand. Measure the temperature inside and outside. Look at the coriander.
Measure again. Compare the coriander. Write what you found and how you would improve the cooler.

projects.record: Each day, write the temperature inside the cooler and outside it. Draw the two coriander bunches side by side.

flow.do: Tell your child about Mohammed Bah Abba and Mansukhbhai Prajapati, and show them the two pots.
flow.say: In the 1990s, a teacher in Nigeria, Mohammed Bah Abba, made a cooler from two clay pots and wet sand. It helped farmers keep vegetables fresh with no electricity. In Gujarat, a potter, Mansukhbhai Prajapati, made a whole clay fridge. Today we build our own.
flow.kid: People found a way to keep food cool without electricity. They used two clay pots and wet sand. Today you will build one!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clay Pot Cooler project. You learn where the idea came from.

flow.do: 1. Put a layer of sand in the bottom of the big pot. 2. Stand the small pot on it. 3. Fill the gap all round with sand. 4. Slowly pour water onto the sand until it is soaked but not flooding. 5. Cover the top with a wet cloth.
flow.say: The sand holds water like a sponge. The water will seep out through the big pot's clay and evaporate.
flow.kid: Put sand in the big pot. Stand the small pot on top. Fill the gap with sand. Pour water on the sand. Cover with a wet cloth.

flow.do: 1. Put one coriander bunch inside the small pot. 2. Put the other in a bowl beside the cooler. 3. After an hour or two, measure the temperature inside the small pot and in the air outside. Write both.
flow.say: One bunch goes in the cooler. Its twin stays outside. That is our fair test.
flow.kid: Put one coriander bunch in the cooler. Put its twin in a bowl outside. Measure inside and outside. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: Measure inside after an hour or two, once the pot has had time to cool. In dry, hot weather, the inside is often 5 to 10 degrees cooler than the air. In sticky monsoon weather it cools less.

flow.do: On day 2, pour more water on the sand. Measure the temperatures again and look at both coriander bunches.
flow.say: The sand has dried a little. Why do we need to add more water?
flow.kid: Pour more water on the sand. Measure inside and outside again. Which coriander looks fresher?

check.q: Why must you keep adding water to the sand?
options: The cooling comes from water evaporating, so it needs a supply of water
The pot gets thirsty
Water makes the pots heavier
check.why: The cooler works because water evaporates from the outside of the big pot, taking heat away. Once the sand dries, there is nothing left to evaporate, and the cooling stops. Picking 'the pot gets thirsty' is a fun way to say it. What the cooler really needs is water in the sand, ready to evaporate.

flow.do: On day 3, measure again, compare the two coriander bunches, and draw both. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Then, how would you improve our cooler?
flow.kid: Measure again. Compare the two bunches. Draw them. Then say what you think, what you saw and why. How would you make your cooler better?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the pot cooler keeps food cooler and fresher. What I saw: inside it was 23 degrees and outside it was 31 degrees. On day 3, the coriander inside was still green. The one outside had wilted. Why: water evaporated from the wet sand and clay, and that took heat away.

challenges.title: Keep the Chai Hot
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a cosy, a warm jacket for a tumbler, from things at home. The cosy that keeps the water hottest after 30 minutes wins.
challenges.problem: A tumbler of hot chai goes cold before Nani gets back to drink it. Design a cosy from home materials that keeps a tumbler of hot water as hot as possible for 30 minutes.
constraints: Use only materials you find at home.
The cosy must come off easily, so someone can drink.
Test it fairly: same tumbler, same amount of hot water, same time.
materials: hot water, poured by a grown-up
home materials such as an old sock, a woollen scarf, newspaper, foil, bubble wrap, cotton wool, a cloth, rubber bands
general: Wrap the tumbler in a thick layer of wool or cloth, which traps air.
Put a lid on top. A lot of heat escapes from the open top.
Put a mat or folded cloth underneath, so heat does not leak into the table.
creative: Use layers, like a spacecraft's shiny blanket and the Ladakh classroom: a shiny layer of foil to reflect heat back, then a fluffy layer to trap air.
Copy a flask. A flask has two walls with almost no air between them. Can you make two walls with a gap?
Copy a bird. Birds fluff their feathers to trap more air. Can you fluff up your material?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cosy. Draw it, build it and test it against a bare tumbler. How many degrees did your cosy save?

flow.do: 1. Explain the challenge. 2. Together, list materials at home that might keep heat in. 3. Your child draws a design.
flow.say: Engineers design first and build second. Which materials do you think will keep the heat in? Why?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Which materials might keep heat in? Draw your cosy design first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Chai Hot. You design a cosy that keeps a tumbler of hot water warm.

flow.do: Build the cosy around one tumbler, leaving room to pour in water.
flow.say: Build it. Remember, someone must be able to take it off to drink.
flow.kid: Build your cosy around one tumbler. Make sure it can come off easily.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours the same amount of hot water into both tumblers. 2. Measure the start temperature. 3. Put the cosy on one tumbler. Leave the other bare. 4. Wait 30 minutes, then measure both.
flow.say: Both start the same. Only one has a cosy. After 30 minutes, which is hotter?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour hot water in both tumblers. Measure them. Put your cosy on one. Wait 30 minutes. Measure both again.

chart.title: Made-up example: water temperature in a bare tumbler and a wrapped tumbler

flow.do: Compare the usual solutions and the creative ideas with your design. Then improve your cosy.
flow.say: How many degrees did your cosy save? What would you change to save even more?
flow.kid: How many degrees warmer was your tumbler? Look at the creative ideas. What would you change?

check.q: Which cosy would keep chai hottest?
options: A thick fluffy woollen one with a lid
A thin sheet of steel wrapped round
No cosy, but a bigger tumbler
check.why: Thick fluffy wool traps lots of still air, which slows heat down. A lid stops heat escaping from the top. A steel wrap is a conductor, so it would carry heat away, not keep it in. Picking 'steel' usually means thinking 'strong' is the property that matters. Here the job needs an insulator.

flow.think: The same cosy could keep a cold drink cold. Why?

challenges.title: Post the Egg
challenges.context: This is a packaging challenge. You must pack a raw egg in a small box so it survives being dropped from a table. You choose the materials, and say why.
challenges.problem: A shop must post fragile things, like glass bangles, without breaking them. Practise with a raw egg. Pack it in a small box so that it does not crack when dropped from table height.
constraints: The box must be small, no bigger than a shoe box.
You can only use materials from home.
Drop it from the same height each time, about the height of a table.
materials: raw eggs (or hard-boiled eggs for practice)
home materials such as newspaper, cotton wool, sponge, rice, cloth, bubble wrap, rubber bands, an old sock
general: Wrap the egg in soft, squashy material, like sponge or cotton wool. It squashes slowly and softens the bump.
Fill all the space in the box, so the egg cannot rattle about and hit the sides.
Crumpled newspaper is cheap and full of air pockets.
creative: Hang the egg in the middle of the box with rubber bands, so it never touches the sides.
Use uncooked rice or dal around the egg, which shifts and spreads out the bump.
Copy nature. Eggs in a nest sit on soft grass and feathers. What could you copy?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own packing. Draw it, pack it and test it. Did your egg survive? What would you change?

flow.do: 1. Explain the problem. 2. Squeeze each material in your hand: sponge, cotton wool, newspaper, rice, cloth. 3. Ask which ones squash softly.
flow.say: Which materials squash softly, like a cushion? Which are hard? Which one would you want around your egg?
flow.kid: Squeeze each material. Which ones squash softly? Which would protect an egg best?
flow.context: This is the first step of Post the Egg. You choose soft materials to protect a raw egg from a fall.

flow.do: Your child packs the egg in a box, using materials they choose. They say why they chose each one.
flow.say: Pack your egg. Tell me why you chose each material.
flow.kid: Pack your egg in a box. Say why you chose each material.

check.q: Why does a squashy material like sponge protect an egg?
options: It squashes slowly, so the egg stops gently instead of suddenly
It is very hard
It is waterproof
check.why: When the box hits the floor, the egg keeps moving. A squashy material lets it slow down gently, over a longer time, so the egg is not hit hard. Picking 'very hard' is the opposite. A hard material would stop the egg suddenly, and it would crack.

flow.do: 1. Spread newspaper on the floor. 2. A grown-up holds the box at table height and drops it. 3. Open it and check the egg. 4. Try again with a better design if it cracked.
flow.say: Three, two, one, drop! Let's open it. Did your egg survive?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to drop your box from table height onto newspaper. Open it. Is the egg safe?
flow.parent: Start with a hard-boiled egg if you want less mess. Wash hands after touching raw egg.

quiz.p: Why do we choose a particular material for a job?
opts: Because its properties suit the job
Because it is the newest material
Because it is the most colourful
Because it is always the cheapest
quiz.why: We look at what the job needs, then find a material with those properties. Picking 'cheapest' is a real thing people think about. But a cheap material that cannot do the job is no use.

quiz.p: Which material is best for a bath towel?
quiz.why: A towel must soak up water, so it needs an absorbent material. Picking plastic means waterproof was taken to mean 'good with water'. A plastic towel would just push the water around.

quiz.p: A kadhai is metal, but its handle is wood. Why?
opts: Metal carries heat to the food. Wood does not carry heat to your hand.
quiz.why: Metal is a conductor of heat, which is right for cooking. Wood is an insulator, which is right for holding. Picking 'wood is stronger' misses the job. The handle is about staying cool, not strength.

quiz.p: In the Hot Spoon Race, which spoon's butter melted first?
opts: They all melted at the same time
quiz.why: Steel is a metal, and metals carry heat quickly up the handle. Picking 'wooden' usually means the result was not yet linked to conductors. The wooden spoon's butter often never melts at all.
quiz.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you put butter on the handle of a steel, a plastic and a wooden spoon, and stand them in hot water.

quiz.p: A steel railing and a wooden bench have been outside all night. The steel feels colder. Why?
opts: Steel carries heat away from your hand faster
quiz.why: They are the same temperature. Steel is a good conductor, so it pulls heat from your hand quickly, and feels colder. Picking 'really colder' trusts the feeling over a thermometer.

quiz.p: Does a woollen sweater make heat?
opts: No. It traps air, which keeps your own heat in.
quiz.why: Wool traps still air, an insulator, which slows your body's heat from escaping. Picking 'wool is always warm' is very common. But an ice cube in a woollen sock melts more slowly, which shows wool makes no heat.
quiz.context: In the sweater and ice cube test, you wrap an ice cube in a woollen sock and leave another bare.

quiz.p: Why does a clay matka keep water cool?
opts: Water seeps through it and evaporates, taking heat away
The water is heavier in clay
quiz.why: Clay is porous, so water reaches the outside and evaporates. Evaporation takes heat away. Picking 'clay is always cold' means thinking a material has its own coldness. A dry clay pot does not cool water.
quiz.context: In the Matka Mystery test, you leave the same water in a clay pot and a plastic bottle side by side, then measure them.

quiz.p: Why is an umbrella made of several materials?
opts: Each material does a different job
Because one material ran out at the factory
quiz.why: Waterproof cloth keeps off rain, springy steel ribs hold it open, and a handle is comfortable to grip. Picking 'one ran out' means thinking the mix is an accident. Designers mix materials on purpose.
quiz.context: In the Take It Apart activity, you look inside an old umbrella and find each material's job.

quiz.p: Bone is made of a bendy material and a hard mineral. Why is this a good design?
opts: Together they make bone hard and tough, not brittle and not floppy
It makes bone soft like jelly
quiz.why: The mineral alone would snap like chalk. The bendy collagen alone would flop. Joined, they make a strong composite. Picking 'heavier' misses the point. The mix is about toughness.

quiz.p: Which is a silly choice of material?
quiz.why: Paper is absorbent and weak when wet, so a paper umbrella would go soggy and tear. Picking 'glass window' might mean worrying that glass breaks. But for a window, being transparent matters most, and glass does that well.

quiz.p: Spectacles for a small child are often plastic, not glass. Why?
opts: Plastic is lighter and does not shatter if dropped
Plastic is always clearer than glass
quiz.why: This is a trade-off. Glass is clear but brittle. Plastic is clear enough, lighter and safer. Picking 'clearer' is a common guess, but good glass is just as clear.

quiz.p: For a feast for 500 people, why might a banana leaf be a better plate than plastic?
opts: It is waterproof on top, cheap, and rots away after use
It lasts for a hundred years
quiz.why: A banana leaf does the plate's job, then goes back into the soil. Thrown-away plastic stays for a very long time. Picking 'lasts a hundred years' gives a property of plastic, which is the problem here.

quiz.p: In the Hot Spoon Race, why must the butter blobs be the same size?
opts: So only the spoon's material changes, which makes it a fair test
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. A smaller blob would melt sooner, even on the same spoon. Picking 'it does not matter' means the result could not be trusted.
quiz.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you put butter on the handle of three spoons and stand them in hot water.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which wrapping kept its ice cube frozen longest?
quiz.why: The sock's bar is tallest, at 95 minutes. Wool trapped air and slowed the room's heat. Picking 'bare plate' usually means the shortest bar was read as 'best'. Here a taller bar means the ice lasted longer.
quiz.context: In the sweater and ice cube test, you wrap ice cubes in different materials and time how long each takes to melt.

chart.title: Minutes until each ice cube melted (made-up results)

quiz.p: Why are metals good at carrying heat?
opts: Some of their electrons move freely and carry energy quickly
quiz.why: Free electrons rush energy through the metal. In wood and plastic, electrons are held in place, so heat creeps along slowly. Picking 'always hot' is the same mix-up as 'metal is colder'. Metals are just at the temperature of their room.

quiz.p: Where were the iron atoms in your steel spoon first made?
quiz.why: Iron atoms were made in stars and in exploding stars, and the explosions scattered them into space. The Earth formed later from that dust. Picking 'factory' is fair, since the spoon was made there. But the factory only shaped iron that was already here.

quiz.p: Scientists copied a lotus leaf to make self-cleaning paint. What is copying nature called?
quiz.why: Biomimicry means copying the clever designs of living things. Picking 'evaporation' mixes it with another word from this unit, which means a liquid turning into a gas.

applications: Cooking pots, tawas and pressure cookers are metal, because metal carries heat to the food.
Pan handles, oven gloves and tea cosies use insulators, like wood, plastic, thick cloth and wool.
Clay matkas and surahis keep water cool, because clay is porous. A clay kulhad is easy to hold with hot chai inside, because clay carries heat slowly.
Electric wires have copper inside to carry electricity, and plastic outside to keep it from reaching your hand.
Windows, spectacles and phone screens use transparent glass or plastic.
Raincoats, umbrellas and tarpaulins use waterproof materials, often cloth coated with plastic or rubber.
Towels, mops, nappies and diya wicks use absorbent materials.
Bridges, buildings and cycle frames use strong steel. Aeroplanes use light aluminium and carbon fibre.
Helmets have a hard plastic shell outside and squashy foam inside, two materials doing two jobs.
Packing for glass and phones uses squashy materials, like bubble wrap, foam and crumpled paper.
Flasks keep tea hot and water cold using two walls with almost no air between them.
Spacecraft, like India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, are wrapped in shiny layered blankets to block the Sun's heat.
Mud houses in Ladakh and Rajasthan use thick walls that soak up heat by day and give it back at night.
Self-cleaning paints and glass copy the bumpy, waxy surface of a lotus leaf.
Doctors use plastic syringes, steel tools and soft cotton, each chosen for a different property.

open_questions.q: Can we make a material that carries electricity with no loss at all, at ordinary room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Some materials do this only when they are extremely cold. Many claims of a room-temperature one, like LK-99 in 2023, failed when others tested them.

open_questions.q: Can we make plastics that last as long as we need them, then safely break down?
open_questions.why_open: Some new plastics do break down, but often only in special hot compost. Scientists are still searching.

open_questions.q: How does a spider make silk so strong, light and tough, at garden temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand parts of it. Making silk just as good in a factory is still very hard.
Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but stuck in place like a solid's. Physicists still argue about how best to explain why some liquids turn into glass when they cool.

open_questions.q: Could buildings one day grow and repair themselves?
open_questions.why_open: Self-healing concrete with bacteria works in tests. Using living materials for whole buildings is still an idea being explored.

open_questions.q: Where did most of the gold on Earth come from?
open_questions.why_open: Exploding stars and crashing neutron stars both make gold. How much comes from each is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Which materials are best for the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how a material is made, how long it is used and what happens to it after. Scientists add these up in different ways, and do not always agree.

maths.problem: In the Hot Spoon Race, the butter on the steel spoon melted after 4 minutes. The butter on the plastic spoon melted after 14 minutes. The wooden spoon's butter had still not melted when the test stopped at 15 minutes. Look at the chart. How many minutes longer did the plastic spoon take than the steel one? What can you say for sure about the wooden spoon?
maths.answer: The plastic spoon took 10 minutes longer. The wooden spoon took at least 11 minutes longer than the steel one, and maybe much more.
maths.explain: The plastic spoon took 14 minutes and the steel spoon took 4. 14 take away 4 is 10. The wooden spoon's butter had not melted at 15 minutes. 15 take away 4 is 11. So the wood took at least 11 minutes longer. We cannot say exactly how much longer, because we stopped watching.
maths.context: In the Hot Spoon Race, you stick butter on the handle of a steel, a plastic and a wooden spoon, stand them in hot water, and time how long each blob takes to melt.

chart.title: Minutes until the butter blob melted (made-up results)
chart.note: The wooden spoon's butter had not melted when the test stopped at 15 minutes.

maths.why_maths: Saying 'steel is faster' is a start. Taking one time away from another tells us how much faster. And when a test stops early, the maths shows what we know for sure and what we do not.

maths.problem: In the sweater and ice cube test, the ice on the bare plate melted in 40 minutes. The ice in the woollen sock lasted 95 minutes. Look at the chart. Put the four wrappings in order, from the one that kept the ice longest to the one that kept it shortest. Then: how many more minutes did the sock's ice last than the bare plate's?
maths.answer: Woollen sock, foil, steel tumbler, bare plate. The sock's ice lasted 55 minutes longer.
maths.explain: Read the height of each bar: sock 95, foil 55, steel tumbler 45, bare plate 40. Put them from biggest to smallest: 95, 55, 45, 40. Then 95 take away 40 is 55. So the sock's ice lasted 55 minutes longer.
maths.context: In the sweater and ice cube test, you wrap same-sized ice cubes in different materials and time how long each takes to melt.

chart.title: Minutes until each ice cube melted (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets you see at a glance which material is the best insulator. Ordering and subtracting tells you how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: Look at the thermometer in the picture. It is standing in the water from the clay matka, after 3 hours on a dry day. Each small mark is 1 degree. What does it read? The water in the plastic bottle read 29 degrees. On a sticky monsoon day, the same test gave 28 degrees in the matka and 29 in the bottle. On which day did the matka cool the water more? Why?
maths.answer: The thermometer reads 24 degrees. On the dry day the matka water was 5 degrees cooler. On the monsoon day it was only 1 degree cooler. The matka cooled more on the dry day, because water evaporates faster into dry air.
maths.explain: Find the top of the coloured line. It is 4 small marks above 20, so it reads 24 degrees. 29 take away 24 is 5. On the monsoon day, 29 take away 28 is 1. 5 is bigger than 1, so the matka cooled more on the dry day. Damp air already holds a lot of water, so less water evaporates from the clay, and less heat is taken away.
maths.context: In the Matka Mystery test, you leave the same water in a clay pot and a plastic bottle side by side for 3 hours, then measure each with a thermometer.

chart.title: A thermometer in the matka water after 3 hours
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 degree.

maths.why_maths: A thermometer is the fair judge in the Matka Mystery, because your hand can be fooled. Comparing two days shows that the cooling depends on the weather, and points to evaporation as the reason.

maths.problem: In the home hunt, a family counted the materials of the objects they found. Plastic: 14. Steel: 9. Cloth: 8. Wood: 6. Glass: 3. How many objects did they find altogether? Which material was found most often?
maths.answer: 40 objects. Plastic was found most often.
maths.explain: Add them up a few at a time. 14 + 9 = 23. 23 + 8 = 31. 31 + 6 = 37. 37 + 3 = 40. The biggest number is 14, for plastic. So plastic was found most often.
maths.context: In the Why Is It Made of That? hunt, you go round your home, write what each object is made of, and keep a tally of each material.

answer_chart.title: Tally of materials found in one home

maths.why_maths: A tally turns a messy hunt into numbers. Adding the numbers and comparing them shows which material your home depends on most.

maths.problem: In the Spoon and Plate Parade, you compared a steel thali and paper plates. One paper plate costs 2 rupees and is used once. A steel thali costs 100 rupees and lasts for years. One person eats one meal a day on a plate. After how many days has that person spent as much on paper plates as on one steel thali?
maths.explain: Each day, one paper plate costs 2 rupees. We need to find how many lots of 2 rupees make 100 rupees. 100 divided by 2 is 50. So after 50 days, the paper plates have cost 100 rupees, the same as the thali. After that, the thali is cheaper every day. You can check: 50 × 2 = 100.
maths.context: In the Spoon and Plate Parade, you line up plates made of different materials and talk about cost and how long each one lasts.

answer_chart.title: Money spent on paper plates, at 2 rupees a day
answer_chart.note: A steel thali costs 100 rupees once. The line reaches 100 rupees on day 50.

maths.why_maths: Durable is a property too. Dividing the cost of the thali by the cost of one paper plate shows how quickly a long-lasting material pays for itself.

roots.context: We have been learning why we choose each material for its job. Now we ask what materials tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A woollen sock squeezed in your fist shrinks to a small lump, because most of it is air. That still air, caught between the fibres, does most of the work of slowing heat. A matka cools water only because its clay has tiny holes that let water seep out and evaporate. So the gaps in a material often do its most important job.
deep_truth.habit: We think a material works because of what it is made of, so we call wool warm and clay cool. But much of the work is done by its gaps, such as the still air between wool's fibres and the tiny holes in baked clay.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sweater test, the ice cube inside a woollen sock lasted about twice as long as a bare one, though wool makes no heat. Squeezed, the same sock shrinks to a small lump, which shows it is mostly air. In the Matka Mystery, the outside of the clay pot is damp, because water seeps out through its pores.

three.who_am_i: Your bones are full of tiny spaces too. The spaces make bone lighter, and it stays strong.
three.what_is_life: Birds fluff up their feathers on cold mornings to hold more still air. Living things used the trapped-air trick long before people did.
three.what_is_this_world: The iron in your spoon was made in stars, long before the Earth formed.

roots.thread: A matka, a sweater and a flask look like solid things. But each one works because of what lies between its parts: tiny holes, pockets of still air, or an empty gap. Everything rises from one source, and the spaces between things belong to that whole as much as the things do. So a material is more than its fibres or its clay. Its gaps are working too.

teachings.teaching: We shape clay into a pot. But it is the empty space inside that makes the pot useful.
teachings.link: The gaps in wool are not truly empty. They are full of still air. But like the space inside Laozi's pot, they are what make the sweater useful. The tiny holes in a matka do the same for cool water.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son that once you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pots are only different shapes and names. What is real is the clay.
teachings.link: A matka, a kulhad and a diya are different objects with different jobs, yet all are clay. This unit's science goes one step further: clay, steel and wool are all atoms, joined in different ways.

science.text: Still air carries heat very poorly. Most good insulators, like wool, feathers, foam and the aerogel used in spacecraft, work by holding air still in tiny spaces.
Iron, and most atoms heavier than helium, were made inside stars. Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle showed how, in 1957.

other_view.who: Democritus, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago
other_view.view: Democritus said there are only atoms and empty space. Hot and cold, sweet and bitter, are only how atoms seem to us. On his view, the gaps are simply empty, and there is no awareness underneath, only atoms moving.

practice.title: Wool and air
practice.say: Hold a woollen sock or shawl loosely in your hands. Breathe in slowly. Now squeeze it into a small ball. Feel how little wool there really is. Breathe out, and let it go. Watch it puff back up as air fills it. Hold it against your cheek. The warmth you feel is your own, held near you by the air.
practice.kid: Hold a woollen sock or shawl. Breathe in. Squeeze it small. Breathe out and let go. Watch it puff up with air. Hold it to your cheek. Whose warmth do you feel?

ask: Is a sweater mostly wool, or mostly air? Which part keeps you warm?
If the gaps do the work, are the gaps part of the material?
Can a thing be useful because of the spaces in it?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people assumed that different materials in the same room held different amounts of cold. It seemed obvious. Touch an iron lock and a woollen blanket on a winter morning, and the iron feels far colder. Joseph Black, a chemist and doctor in Scotland, showed that this is wrong. In his lectures, from the 1760s, he taught that things left together in a room without a fire, such as iron, wood, wool and water, all end up at the same temperature. A thermometer placed on each one shows the same reading. Heat always spreads from warmer things to cooler ones until they are equal. So why does the iron feel colder? Your hand is warmer than the room. Iron carries heat away from your hand quickly, so your skin cools fast. Wool carries heat away slowly, so your hand stays warm. Black died in 1799. His friend John Robison published his lectures in 1803, so that others could learn from them.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Black, a Scottish chemist and doctor
how_we_found_out.when: from the 1760s (his lectures were published in 1803)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Different materials in the same room are at different temperatures: iron is colder than wood or wool. Thermometers show they are all the same. Iron only feels colder because it carries heat away from your hand faster.
